note: Issue-filing view of the 2026-08-07 Python audit (open_python-audit.md). High and medium findings carry their full `why` + `recommendation`; low findings are index-only (title + sites), since the markdown carries the same one-liner. The verifier's `evidence` and `verify_note` prose was dropped to stay inside the repo's 500 KB file policy — re-run the audit workflow to regenerate the full form. The epic map (E1-E12) is in the markdown, not here.

findings.title: endpoints/stores.py raises service_kit.exceptions, which bypass the catalog's RFC 9457 problem handler entirely
findings.why: Every other error in this service carries the spec's numeric `code` and the `application/problem+json` media type; generated Lance-Namespace clients dispatch on that `code`. Three routes in `/v1/stores` answer a differently-shaped body with no `code` at all, so a client that parses the catalog's documented error model gets a parse failure or a silent fall-through on exactly the conflict/unavailable paths it must handle. It also fires the default FastAPI `HTTPException` handler, which is the one path `install_problem_handlers` was written to remove.
findings.recommendation: Replace the three `service_kit.exceptions` raises with their `lance_namespace` equivalents (`NamespaceAlreadyExistsError` for the duplicate-name conflict, `InvalidInputError` for the missing name/bucket, `ServiceUnavailableError` from `lance_namespace` for the unreadable/absent state store) and drop the `service_kit.exceptions` import. Add a contract test asserting `content-type == application/problem+json` and a present `code` on a duplicate `POST /v1/stores`.

findings.title: GET /v1/stores and /v1/stores/tiers disclose the whole estate's buckets and hosts with no authorization gate, while the sibling POST calls that same set estate-wide disclosure
findings.why: The read of an estate-wide fact is ungated while the write of the same fact is estate-admin gated — the asymmetry means any authenticated principal (any project member) enumerates every object store the estate knows, including `endpoint` hosts of attached third-party buckets. The three comparable estate-wide surfaces all gate or filter: `/v1/events` (`require_relation` can_observe_events), `/v1/projects` (same), `/v1/warehouses` (`fga.list_objects` filter). This is the systemic hazard of the `{id}`-keyed router guard: ~30 routes whose path param is not literally `id` (`{warehouse_id}`, `{project_id}`, `{model}`) or which have none at all rely entirely on a hand-written in-handler gate, and these two were written without one.
findings.recommendation: Gate both reads on `can_observe_events` against `settings.fga_root_object` exactly as `attach_store` does (or FGA-filter per store if a narrower tier is wanted), and add a test that an authenticated non-estate-admin gets 403 from `GET /v1/stores`. Separately, add a contract test that enumerates every mounted route and asserts each one either matches a `_RESOURCES` prefix (router-gated) or names an explicit `require_relation`/`require_can_*` call — so the next ungated estate surface fails a test rather than shipping.

findings.title: Multi-step orchestration lives in endpoint functions instead of services/, despite the service having a services/ layer
findings.why: The chosen layout (fastapi-template, layout (b)) puts business logic in `services/` and leaves endpoints routing-only; this is a violation *within* the service's own chosen layout, which the house rules call out explicitly. Concretely it costs testability — `create_table`'s compensation arm carries an in-code note that it is unreachable in the moto harness because it needs FGA on, which is a direct consequence of the logic being reachable only through HTTP — and it costs reuse: the identical drop→trash→clear-protection→emit→revoke sequence is hand-rolled three times (table drop, namespace cascade, warehouse cascade) rather than being one service function.
findings.recommendation: Move each orchestration into `catalog/services/` as a plain async function taking the already-resolved collaborators (`ns`, `so`, settings, fga client, emitters) and returning a result model; leave the handler as parse-id → call service → shape response. Start with the two highest-value pairs: a `services/tables.py::drop_table`/`rename_table` and a `services/hierarchy.py::cascade_drop` shared by `namespaces.drop_namespace` and `warehouses.delete_warehouse`. This unblocks unit tests for the FGA-on compensation and cascade paths without an HTTP client.

findings.title: Endpoint modules import each other's private helpers, and one imports a private helper out of api/dependencies
findings.why: Endpoints are the outermost layer; nothing should import *from* one. `_has_external_bases` is multi-base data-plane logic that opens a Lance dataset — it belongs in `services/dataplane.py`, and routing it through `credentials.py` means a change to the vending endpoint silently changes `describe_table`'s behaviour. `UserStateStoreDep` is a shared dependency living in an endpoint module. `_namespace_for_root` is explicitly marked private by PEP-8 convention and is reached across a module boundary, which the code-style rules call a smell in exactly this direction: either it is public (drop the underscore and document it) or the caller should not reach in.
findings.recommendation: Move `_has_external_bases` and its `lance.dataset` sibling `_current_version` into `catalog/services/dataplane.py` and import both endpoints from there. Move `get_user_state_store`/`UserStateStoreDep` into `api/dependencies.py` alongside the other deps. Rename `_namespace_for_root` to `namespace_for_root` (it is already public API for two callers) or expose it through a small `WarehouseNamespaceDep`.

findings.title: Eleven wire schemas are defined inline in endpoint modules although schemas.py declares itself the single home — the exact drift its docstring cites a bug for
findings.why: The rule and the hazard are both already written down in this codebase; eleven models sit on the wrong side of it. Any future duplicate name between two endpoint modules reproduces the exact OpenAPI-name-mangling regression that motivated `schemas.py` in the first place, and `tests/unit/test_openapi_contract.py` would only catch it after a client had already been generated against the mangled name.
findings.recommendation: Move all eleven into `schemas.py` under the existing section banners (a Warehouse/Project/Identity/Events section already exists or is trivially added). `UserStateEnvelope[T]` is generic and can move unchanged. Then add an assertion to `test_openapi_contract.py` that no schema name in `/openapi.json` contains `__`.

findings.title: Three tuple write/revoke call sites bypass the seed_ownership/revoke_ownership seam, each for a documented reason
_collect_descendants recurses with no depth cap and no cycle guard, while its sibling enumerator in the same service has both
Bare `except Exception` around seed_ownership makes any programming error in the grant path look like an FGA outage
The estate-gate / audit-on-outage preamble is hand-copied across eleven handlers and reaches into app.state.fga instead of using the existing FgaClientDep
findings.why: Eleven copies of an audit-and-fail-closed preamble is eleven places to forget one on the next surface — and `fga_deps.py:79` already records that exact bug class ("Unmapped it would fall to WRITER, which is how the live audit found it"). Bypassing `FgaClientDep` and `ControlEmitterDep` also defeats `dependency_overrides` in tests, which is why these handlers are tested through `app.state` monkeypatching rather than the supported seam.
findings.recommendation: Turn `_estate_gate` into a real dependency — `EstateFgaDep = Annotated[OpenFgaClient, Depends(estate_gate)]` composing `FgaClientDep` + `SettingsDep` + `CurrentToken` — and declare it on the `/v1/access` router via `APIRouter(..., dependencies=[...])` or on each handler. Extract the audit preamble into one `@asynccontextmanager audited(event, subject, resource)` that emits FAILURE-on-`ServiceUnavailableError` and SUCCESS on clean exit, and use it at all 11 sites. Inject `ControlEmitterDep` in `_mutate_tuple` and `_access_mutate` instead of calling `get_control_emitter(request)`.

findings.title: Two sibling access surfaces map the same client error to different spec codes — 501 UnsupportedOperation vs 400 InvalidInput for an unknown relation name
findings.why: A caller-supplied relation name that the model does not define is a malformed request, not a capability the server lacks. Returning 501 tells a generated client and every retry policy that the *operation* is unimplemented — so a client will stop calling the endpoint entirely rather than fixing its input — and it lands the request in the `unsupported_operation` log stream, where it is indistinguishable from a genuine backend stub. The two surfaces validating the same model in the same service disagreeing means whichever one a client integrates against first sets its wrong expectation.
findings.recommendation: Change the three `UnsupportedOperationError` raises in `access.py` that reject caller-supplied relation names to `InvalidInputError`, matching `access_admin.py`. Keep `UnsupportedOperationError` only for the genuinely-unsupported case already in those handlers (`"access review requires OpenFGA (this stack runs auth-off)"`). Add a test asserting a bad relation yields 400 on both `/v1/table/{id}/access/check` and `/v1/access/check`.

findings.title: Cascade and enumeration paths await independent object-store I/O one item at a time
findings.why: These are independent per-object round trips to S3/OpenFGA, serialised. On the read path (`list_all_tables`) the estate listing pays one full round trip per bound namespace, which is the endpoint a UI hits on every page load. On the destructive paths a large subtree turns a single cascade into hundreds of serial S3 GETs, and the request is the one holding the caller's timeout — the same failure mode `projects.py` already fixed with `gather` for a much cheaper lookup. Ordering only genuinely matters for the drop loops (deepest-first); the guard/enumeration/revoke loops have no ordering constraint at all.
findings.recommendation: `asyncio.gather` the order-independent loops: the protection sweep in `_require_descendants_unprotected`, the descendant `revoke_ownership` and `clear_protection` loops in `drop_namespace`, and the per-binding listing in `list_all_tables` (bounded with a semaphore if the estate is large). Leave the deepest-first drop loops sequential and say so in a comment, so the distinction is deliberate rather than incidental.

findings.title: The batch authorizer loops sequential fga.check calls for owner-tier operations instead of batch_check
findings.why: House rule 12 names this exactly: a loop of N sequential `check()` calls where `batch_check` costs one round trip. It sits on the authorization hot path of `POST /v1/table/batch-commit`, before any work is done, so a batch of K deregisters pays K serial OpenFGA round trips while the writer-tier objects in the *same* request are batched. The in-code justification ("per-object keeps the per-op relation exact") is satisfied by grouping: `_BATCH_OWNER_OPS` is a small dict, so one `batch_check` per distinct relation preserves exactness.
findings.recommendation: Group `owner_checks` by relation and issue one `fga.batch_check` per distinct relation (today that is a single call, since `_BATCH_OWNER_OPS` has one entry), then emit the per-object audit rows from the returned map exactly as the two branches above already do.

findings.title: services/catalog/tests is missing from the explicit pytest testpaths, so five tests never run
findings.why: The house rules note that testpaths are explicit, not discovered — which makes an omitted directory silently invisible rather than a collection error. Five tests guarding a data-duplication contract have never gated a commit, and the file's existence makes it look covered to anyone reading the tree.
findings.recommendation: Add `"services/catalog/tests"` to `testpaths` and run the suite; if the tests are stale, fix or delete them rather than leaving them uncollected. Consider a meta-test that asserts every `services/*/tests` and `packages/*/tests` directory on disk appears in `testpaths`, so the next service to add tests cannot be silently skipped.

findings.title: user_state.py and policies.py ship near-identical handler triples, four and three times over
Annotated-Depends aliases are used as plain parameter annotations on functions that are not dependencies
Constrained string values are passed as bare `str | None` and re-parsed with ad-hoc .lower() comparisons instead of StrEnum
The lifespan mutates the @lru_cache'd Settings singleton in place to inject the S3 secret
An async route performs uncached blocking file I/O to read the authorization model DSL
create_table runs a parent-existence round trip before the cheap request-shape validations it should follow
Two task-listing routes declare a CurrentToken dependency their bodies never use
Commit idempotency guard fails OPEN on any storage error, re-enabling the duplicate-append it exists to prevent
findings.why: This is the one guard standing between a Dapr activity replay and duplicated bronze rows; `services/catalog/tests/test_commit_idempotency.py:9-10` records that the sibling hole was measured at "nine copies per file". Append never conflicts with Append, so nothing downstream refuses the duplicate — a single transient read failure during a retry silently corrupts the table's row count. The per-version `continue` has the same shape: a transient failure reading OUR OWN marker version skips it and the replay appends again.
findings.recommendation: Discriminate: treat only a genuinely-absent dataset (`FileNotFoundError` / lance's "was not found" message shape, the discrimination `read_blob` already performs at dataplane.py:804-815) as "no prior commit"; let every other exception propagate as `ServiceUnavailableError` so the caller retries rather than duplicating. Same for the per-version read: skip only on a missing/GC'd transaction file, propagate on a store error. Add a test that injects a raising storage layer and asserts the commit is refused, not duplicated.

findings.title: STS session policy is built by unescaped interpolation — a wildcard in a table name widens vended credentials to sibling tables
findings.why: This defeats the isolation the suite explicitly asserts — `tests/unit/test_vending.py:216 test_a_policy_does_not_reach_a_SIBLING_table_in_the_same_bucket` — and the suite's own `_policy_allows` helper (line 181-191) documents that "`*` in a Resource arn matches any run of characters — the same wildcard the store applies", so the wildcard semantics are known but never tested against a name that carries one. A caller who may create a table (the default `fga_lock_root_create=False` posture lets any authenticated caller create at top level) can name it to widen its own vended write-tier credentials over neighbours' data. Reachable in `sts` and `web_identity` modes; `mode_b` (the default) vends nothing, and an FGA-enabled deployment may independently reject such an id at ownership-seed time — but the defect is the unescaped interpolation into a security boundary, which no deployment posture fixes.
findings.recommendation: Reject or escape IAM-significant characters (`*`, `?`) in `build_session_policy` before interpolation — raise `InvalidInputError` rather than vending a widened policy — and apply a segment charset rule at `parse_identifier` so an unvendable name cannot be created in the first place. Separately reconsider the empty-prefix branch: it grants the whole bucket, which `test_build_session_policy_root_prefix` (test_vending.py:48-51) currently asserts as intended, but a location that unexpectedly resolves to the bucket root should refuse rather than widen. Add a test with `*` in the table name asserting the sibling-isolation property still holds.

findings.title: The catalog's in-service test directory is not in `testpaths`, so the commit-idempotency tests never run in CI
findings.why: House rule 1: testpaths are EXPLICIT, so a test directory that is not listed is invisible. These five tests are the only automated protection on the replay guard whose failure mode the same file documents as "nine copies per file" — the tests are green and simply never asked to run. Any regression in `_find_run_commit` or `commit_appended_fragments` ships silently.
findings.recommendation: Add `"services/catalog/tests"` to `testpaths` in the root `pyproject.toml`. While there, audit the remaining `services/*/tests` directories for the same omission — the listed set covers five services and the estate has more.

findings.title: `dataplane.py` is a 1438-line God module carrying twelve unrelated concerns, including HTTP protocol semantics
findings.why: House rule 6 names "God modules (1000+ line files mixing concerns)" as a flag within a sanctioned layout. The practical cost is real: any change to tag handling reloads the commit-conflict taxonomy and the Arrow type table into a reader's head, and the file's twelve concerns have no reason to change together. The HTTP-range logic in particular means the service layer cannot be reasoned about without RFC 9110.
findings.recommendation: Split into a `services/dataplane/` package along the existing seams: `create.py`, `relocate.py`, `commit.py`, `blobs.py`, `errors.py` (the `_user_sql`/`_column_op` translators + their regexes), `schema_ops.py`, `refs.py` (tags + branches), `history.py`. Keep the public function names so endpoints need only their import lines changed. Move the Range/If-Range resolution out of `read_blob` into the endpoint (or a small `http_range.py`) so the service returns a blob handle + size and the HTTP layer owns the protocol.

findings.title: Control-plane registry writes are plain overwrites with no compare-and-swap — concurrent updates are silently lost
findings.why: The catalog runs multiple replicas (the control-event subscription is explicitly a broadcast so "every replica receives every event"). A deactivate racing a re-create, or two field updates on the same warehouse/project record, silently drop one writer's change — and `put_project`'s docstring says it "carries mutable lifecycle fields (`protected`) forward on a re-create", which is exactly the read-modify-write that loses a concurrent `protected` flip. `warehouses.py:141` states "A binding is immutable... so a resolver may cache it forever" — bindings are safe, but the mutable records sharing this primitive are not.
findings.recommendation: Give `_write_json` a conditional-write mode: read the object's ETag/version alongside the record and PUT with `If-Match` (S3 conditional writes), retrying the read-modify-write on a 412. Route `set_warehouse_status` and any `put_*` that carries fields forward through it; leave the genuinely create-only writes (bindings) on the unconditional path. Add a concurrency test asserting a lost update is detected rather than silently applied.

findings.title: The model registry collapses every `OSError` to 404, reporting a store outage as "model not found"
findings.why: A RustFS/S3 5xx, a credential failure or a timeout is reported to the console and to generated clients as a 404 problem+json. Clients do not retry a 404, the models page renders "not found" during an outage, and an operator debugging it chases a missing registry instead of a broken store. It also mis-gates promotion: `promote`'s existence check turns a transient outage into a permanent-looking refusal.
findings.recommendation: Discriminate as `read_blob` and `_classify_commit_error` already do in this service: map only the "dataset at path … was not found" / "_versions/N.manifest was not found" message shapes to `TableNotFoundError` / `TableVersionNotFoundError`, and raise `ServiceUnavailableError` for everything else so the 503 reaches the client. Factor the discrimination into one shared helper rather than a third copy.

findings.title: An 11-keyword emitter signature is hand-copied seven times across the lineage emission layer
findings.why: House rule 14 (">3 params → a model") and DRY-as-knowledge: adding one field to a lineage event today means editing seven signatures, and a miss in `NoopEmitter` or the Protocol is a type error nobody sees until the off-state path runs. The `ControlEmitter` sibling in `control_emit.py:46` shows the right shape in the same package — `async def emit(self, event: CatalogControlEvent) -> None` — a single-argument Pydantic payload.
findings.recommendation: Mirror `control_emit.py`: define a Pydantic `WriteEvent` model with those eleven fields and reduce the Protocol to `async def emit(self, event: WriteEvent) -> None`. Drop `emit_create` entirely (callers pass `operation=CREATE_TABLE`) or keep exactly one convenience wrapper on the base class. This collapses ~120 lines to ~25 and makes the payload validatable.

findings.title: Service functions return `dict[str, Any]` that endpoints splat into Pydantic models, so the boundary is unchecked
findings.why: House rule 2 (Pydantic for structured values) and house rule 3 (annotate public signatures). Renaming a key in `preview_gc`'s return dict is a silent runtime `TypeError` at the endpoint rather than a type-check failure, and a reader of the service function has to open `schemas.py` to learn the shape. `ty` runs with `error-on-warning = true` and gets nothing from this boundary.
findings.recommendation: Have the service functions construct and return the existing Pydantic models directly (`preview_gc(...) -> GcPreview`), and let the endpoints return them unchanged. For `models.describe`/`summarize`/`list_artifacts` and `dataplane.table_history`, introduce the corresponding models — several already exist (`ModelSummary` at schemas.py:538).

findings.title: Each mutating table op performs three full namespace describes plus three dataset opens
findings.why: Every one of these is an object-store round trip on the write path, occupying a threadpool worker (Starlette's default budget is 40) for the whole duration. The mutation already holds an open, post-commit dataset handle whose `.version` is current; the third open exists only to re-read the version and schema the second open could have returned. Under concurrent writes this triples the store load and the tail latency for no information gain.
findings.recommendation: Have the mutating functions return `(response, dataset)` or read `dataset.version` off the handle they already hold instead of calling `_version`, and let `read_version_and_schema` accept an already-open dataset so `emit_measured_write` reuses it. Keep `_version`'s branch-correctness contract (its docstring is right that the branch must match) — the fix is reuse, not removal.

findings.title: The commit path issues unbounded serial object-store round trips — one HEAD per data file, one transaction read per version
findings.why: Both sit on the hot governed-write path inside a threadpool worker. A distributed write staging a few hundred fragments pays hundreds of serialized HEAD requests before the commit even starts; the docstring's bound is an assumption about caller behaviour, not a property of the code, and nothing enforces it.
findings.recommendation: Collect the relative paths and issue a single `fs.get_file_info(paths)` batch call, then diff for `NotFound`. Bound the replay scan explicitly — cap it at the last N versions (or reject a `read_version` further than N behind current with a clear 400) and correct the docstring, which currently asserts a guarantee the code does not provide. Also extract the `(frag.get("files") if isinstance(frag, dict) else None) or []` expression into a named helper; it requires mental execution to read.

findings.title: The warehouse registry hand-rolls a raw boto3 S3 client instead of the canonical `packages/storage` wrapper
findings.why: House rule 8 makes `packages/storage` the single canonical S3 wrapper, and the standing memory ruling is that storage must stay MinIO/HCP/AWS-agnostic through env settings, never a code change. A second hand-built client is where that agnosticism drifts: this one hardcodes its own `us-east-1` fallback and omits the addressing-style and TLS handling the wrapper centralizes, so a backend the wrapper supports can still fail here.
findings.recommendation: Add `storage` to the catalog's dependencies and have `_bucket_client` delegate to `storage.s3_client(...)`, passing the catalog's `storage_options` through as the explicit credential override the wrapper already accepts. `provision_bucket` and `purge_bucket` then need no change.

findings.title: Three object-store registries parse JSON into raw dicts and hand-validate with `.get()` truthiness checks
findings.why: House rule 2 (Pydantic for structured values) and the "missing input validation at boundaries" anti-pattern: JSON read off object storage is external data, and the field set each consumer requires is encoded three times in three ad-hoc truthiness expressions that have already diverged (warehouse records check three fields, bindings two, projects one). There is no single place that says what a warehouse record IS.
findings.recommendation: Define `WarehouseRecord`, `NamespaceBinding` and `ProjectRecord` Pydantic models; have `_read_json`/`_write_json` become generic over a model (`model_validate_json` on read, `model_dump_json` on write) so a malformed record raises `ValidationError` and the existing skip-with-warning tolerance catches exactly that one exception instead of `Exception`. The `status`/`protected` lifecycle fields then get declared defaults rather than `record.get("status") or "active"`.

findings.title: A single 340-line `Settings` class carries every domain's configuration
findings.why: The fastapi skill names this exactly — "One `BaseSettings` for the whole app → every domain reads every var; nothing is scoped" — and the practical consequence is visible: `SettingsDep` is injected into endpoints that need one field and receive the S3 secret, the FGA store id and the vending role ARN along with it, and any module that touches config imports all sixty fields. It also makes the file the single busiest merge point in the service.
findings.recommendation: Split into per-domain `BaseSettings` groups (`StorageConfig`, `OidcConfig`, `FgaConfig`, `VendingConfig`, `LineageConfig`, `ControlConfig`, `LimitsConfig`) composed on one root `Settings`, keeping the `LANCE_*` aliases byte-identical so nothing in the chart changes. Move each `@model_validator` next to the fields it validates. `get_settings`'s `@lru_cache` and the fail-fast posture stay as they are — both are correct.

findings.title: The project registry imports two private helpers across a module boundary
Maintenance ops type their dataset parameter as `Any` where a small Protocol would state the contract (style, not a gate violation)
`@dataclass` value object and a duplicated legacy type alias in the data plane
`create_table` is a 36-line pass-through that forwards every argument to `_create_table_direct`
The OpenLineage `producer` URI stamped on every emitted event points at the wrong repository and a non-existent path
Workflow control flow branches on import-time os.getenv values — a replay on a pod with different env changes the recorded task sequence
findings.why: dapr-workflows.md's determinism table lists `os.environ[...]` reads as a workflow-function prohibition: "Pass via input or activity". A workflow replays from history on whichever pod picks it up. If a rolling restart, a `kubectl set env`, or a values change moves `RASK_INGEST_MAX_RUN_HOURS` between 0 and non-zero while a run is in flight, the replay either creates a durable timer the history has no record of, or skips one the history has — a task-sequence divergence, which is the exact class of change that wedges a durable workflow permanently. `MAX_UNITS` has the milder version: the same run reports FAILED-by-ceiling or COMPLETE depending on which pod replayed it. This plane already knows the rule — `sizing` is documented as "resolved ONCE, at accept, and carried" precisely so "a rolling restart cannot change a live run's fragment size mid-fan-out" — and then leaves the two ceilings, and sizing's own fallback path, outside that discipline.
findings.recommendation: Resolve both ceilings at ACCEPT (`api.create_ingest`, where `sizing` is already resolved) and carry them as required fields on `RunSpec`; read them from `spec` inside the workflow, never from module state. Make `sizing` a required field on `RunSpec`/`ChunkSpec` rather than `default_factory=resolve`, so no env read is reachable from a workflow-body `model_validate`; keep the compat default only behind an explicit accept-time migration. Add a test that runs `ingest_run` twice over the same recorded history with the env changed between and asserts the yielded task sequence is identical.

findings.title: Three of four NATS connect sites have no timeout, against the file's own measured evidence that a connect to a dead broker never returns
findings.why: These three sites are the bodies of the `publish_units`, `drain_chunk` and `reconcile_chunk` ACTIVITIES. A Dapr activity has no execution timeout, so an unreachable or slow-to-DNS broker hangs the activity indefinitely: `ACTIVITY_RETRY` never fires (nothing raised), the child workflow never returns, the parent's `when_all` never completes, and the run sits RUNNING forever with no error anywhere. The one place a bound exists is the tidy-up path, which is the least important of the four. Resilience guidance is "timeouts everywhere — every network call"; here the plane measured the failure, wrote the fix, and applied it to one call.
findings.recommendation: Put the bound inside the seam: give `WorkQueue.connect` an explicit `connect_timeout` / `max_reconnect_attempts` and wrap it in `asyncio.wait_for` there, so every caller inherits it and no future call site can forget. Give the drain a separate, larger overall deadline (it legitimately runs long) but keep the CONNECT bounded at seconds. Add a test that points `RASK_NATS_URL` at a black-hole address and asserts each activity raises within the bound rather than hanging.

findings.title: discover_staged's exact-cover search is super-linear in the run's whole unit universe and recurses once per fragment — it cannot finish the million-unit run this plane advertises
findings.why: The module's own scale statement is a million-unit harvest (`workflow.py` docstring, `CHUNK_SIZE = 1000`). A 1M-unit run stages ~1000 manifests over a 1,000,000-key universe: the FIRST search node builds a million-entry dict, each doing ~1000 subset tests of ~1000 elements — that call does not return. Even the benign no-overlap case, which picks one fragment per node, recurses to depth ≈ number of fragments, so ~1000+ staged fragments hits Python's default recursion limit and raises `RecursionError` — inside `finalize_run`, the single commit point for the whole run, after every byte has already been fetched and staged. `_SEARCH_NODE_LIMIT` returning `None` is worse, not better: `discover_staged` translates it into `StagingOverlapError` ("no selection covers every unit exactly once"), so a run that had a perfectly clean cover is refused as if it were corrupt.
findings.recommendation: Index once instead of rescanning: build `unit -> [fragment index]` and a per-fragment remaining-count, then run the cover iteratively (explicit stack, no recursion). Short-circuit the overwhelmingly common case first — if the staged unit sets are pairwise disjoint, the cover is all of them, no search needed. Scope the cover per CHUNK rather than per run (staging roots are already per run; adding the chunk segment makes each search a handful of fragments by construction), and bound by unit count, not node count. Add a scale test with 1000+ manifests over 10^5 units asserting `discover_staged` returns in bounded time and does not raise.

findings.title: The run-deadline path abandons its child workflows and then purges the queue underneath them
findings.why: On the deadline path the parent declares the run FAILED while every unfinished `chunk_run` child is still durably executing — each still inside `drain_chunk`, fetching from the source and writing Lance fragments against `dataset_uri`. `release_run_units` then purges the run's subject and deletes the shared durable consumer out from under those live pull subscriptions, so in-flight acks and fetches fail against a consumer that no longer exists. The fragments those children already staged are never collected: `purge_staged` runs only inside `finalize_run`, which the timeout path deliberately skips. The net state is orphaned children still hammering a rate-limited source for a run nobody will commit, plus staged bytes with no owner — which is precisely the "unreclaimable orphan" condition `release_run` was written to prevent, reintroduced one layer up. The comment at :299-301 claims "the staged fragments stay staged — recoverable by a re-run", but a re-run gets a new `run_id`, hence a new staging root, so nothing ever reads them.
findings.recommendation: On the deadline (and any early-terminal) path, terminate the outstanding child workflow instances before emitting terminal — `ctx` cannot do it, so pass the child instance ids out to a `terminate_children` activity that uses `DaprWorkflowClient.terminate_workflow`, and only release the queue once they are quiescent. At minimum, make `release_run_units` a no-op when children may still be live, and make `purge_staged(uri, run_id)` run on every terminal path (not only inside `finalize_run`) so abandoned fragments are reclaimed rather than orphaned.

findings.title: Transient fetch failures nak with no delay and max_deliver exhaustion is never detected — the DLQ the module docstring promises is unreachable for the common failure
findings.why: Two gaps. (1) `nak()` with no delay is immediate redelivery — a tight retry loop against the rate-limited external endpoint that `max_ack_pending` and `fetch_concurrency` exist to be gentle with. `background-jobs.md` uses `await msg.nak(delay=2 ** attempts)` for exactly this. (2) A unit that fails transiently three times is never parked and never named: JetStream stops delivering it, so it is not in `outcome.errors`, and the drain's completion predicate never reaches `expected` — the loop spins to the 30s fetch timeout and breaks, `reconcile_chunk` reports a bare `"N units still outstanding"`, and the operator gets a count with no unit key and no DLQ entry. The docstring's promise that poison "leaves the queue and parks" holds only for permanent-status and validation failures, which are the two cases the code already handles synchronously — never for the exhausted-transient case the DLQ was justified by.
findings.recommendation: Use `msg.nak(delay=...)` with exponential backoff derived from `msg.metadata.num_delivered`. Before naking, check `num_delivered >= MAX_DELIVER` and take the terminal branch instead: record the unit in `outcome.errors` with the last exception, `park_poison`, then `msg.term()` (or `ack()`) so the unit leaves the stream named rather than silently stuck. Add a test that fails a fetch `MAX_DELIVER` times and asserts a DLQ publish and a named entry in `ChunkOutcome.errors`.

findings.title: park_poison publishes unguarded — one bad unit fails the whole run when the DLQ stream is absent
findings.why: A JetStream publish to a subject with no stream raises (`NoStreamResponseError` / no responders). That exception propagates out of `handle`, out of the `asyncio.gather(*(handle(m) for m in fresh))`, out of `drain_chunk`, into Dapr, which burns all four `ACTIVITY_RETRY` attempts against a permanently-failing condition and then fails the whole run. So in any environment where the chart Job has not run — every local run, every test cluster brought up without it, and the window before the Job completes — a single corrupt TIFF or a single 404 page turns a recoverable "one unit refused" into a total run failure. That is the opposite of the design intent stated three lines above the call: "one request, one verdict, named in `errors`".
findings.recommendation: Make parking best-effort at the seam, the same way `release_run` already is: wrap the publish in `park_poison` and log at WARNING on failure, returning a bool so the caller can record "parked" vs "dropped" in the unit's error string. Have `ensure_stream()` also ensure the DLQ stream (or explicitly document it as chart-owned and surface its absence in `/queue` as unhealthy rather than a log line).

findings.title: No trace context crosses the queue boundary; UnitTask.traceparent is a declared-but-never-written field
findings.why: `python-infrastructure/observability.md` § "Trace context across queue boundaries": "Publishing to NATS JetStream loses the current trace unless you propagate it explicitly via message headers… Without context propagation, distributed traces stop at every queue boundary." That is exactly the state here — the API's span, the workflow's activities, and the worker's fetch/validate/write are three disconnected traces, so nobody can follow one page from `POST /v1/ingests` to the fragment it landed in. The declared field makes it worse than a plain omission: it reads as a working mechanism (its own description asserts the property), so a reader checking whether propagation exists finds a field and stops looking.
findings.recommendation: At publish, `propagate.inject(carrier)` and either set the carrier as the NATS headers alongside `Nats-Msg-Id` or fill `UnitTask.traceparent`; at consume, `ctx = propagate.extract(...)` and open the per-unit span under it. If propagation is not going to be implemented now, delete the field rather than leaving a description that asserts a property the code does not have.

findings.title: Every chunk's reconcile error uses the literal key "__chunk__", and the parent flattens all chunks into one dict — N failures collapse to one
findings.why: `errors` is keyed by unit key everywhere else, so a run where 40 of 1000 chunks each reconcile short reports ONE error entry — whichever chunk the comprehension visited last — and the count in it is that chunk's alone. The run then reports `COMPLETE_WITH_ERRORS` with a single message that understates the damage by orders of magnitude, and the operator has no way to know which chunks are short. `error-handling.md` § batch processing exists for exactly this: partial failures must be tracked per item, not collapsed. Related loss at :373: `ChunkResult.model_validate({k: v for k, v in drained.items() if k in ChunkResult.model_fields})` drops `units_done`, so the parent never sees per-chunk progress either.
findings.recommendation: Key the reconcile error by chunk — `{f"__chunk__:{chunk.chunk_id}": ...}` — or return a structured `errors: dict[str, str]` where the key is the chunk id. Add `units_done` to `ChunkResult` so the parent can report actual vs expected per chunk. Add a test that fans out two short chunks and asserts both appear in the run's `errors`.

findings.title: Operational tunables read via scattered os.getenv with no settings singleton — the plane already uses pydantic-settings for auth but not for NATS/S3/warehouse/queue config, and queue numbers are duplicated in the chart
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-9 and `configuration.md` § "Import a singleton — don't `os.getenv` throughout the codebase": scattered reads mean nothing validates types or ranges at startup, nothing fails fast on a typo'd var, and no single place documents what this service consumes. Two concrete consequences already visible in the code: the workflow's env reads are the determinism hazard in finding 01, and the code/chart duplication is a correctness relation the plane can only warn about after the fact (`_warn_if_retention_disagrees`) rather than assert at boot.
findings.recommendation: Add one `pydantic-settings` `BaseSettings` for the plane (`RASK_INGEST_*` + `RASK_NATS_URL` + `RASK_S3_ENDPOINT_URL`) behind an `@lru_cache get_settings()`, and have every module read it. Validate the cross-field relations there at startup — `fragment_rows < max_ack_pending`, `ack_wait > heartbeat`, dedupe window matching the chart — so a misconfiguration is a startup failure with a message rather than a mid-run deadlock or a silent retention mismatch.

findings.title: drain_chunk and finalize_run are oversized multi-purpose functions with nested closures and a coroutine redefined inside a loop
findings.why: `design-patterns.md` § Function size: extract when a function exceeds 20-50 lines, serves multiple distinct purposes, or nests 3+ levels. All three qualify on every criterion. In `drain_chunk` specifically the nesting is load-bearing rather than cosmetic — the module's own comments record two bugs caused by it (the heartbeat closing over a rebound `pending_msgs`, and `held` needing to be a never-reassigned dict), which is what a five-`nonlocal` closure pair costs. `handle` being re-created per loop iteration is pure noise that also makes the concurrency shape harder to see.
findings.recommendation: Extract the open batch into a small class (`_Batch` holding `units/parts/msgs/bytes` with `add()` and `flush()`), so `drain_chunk` becomes fetch → partition fresh/redelivered → batch.add / batch.flush and the `nonlocal` chain disappears. Hoist `handle` out of the loop as a method taking the batch. Split `finalize_run` into `_select_fragments`, `_commit(catalog, …)` (one function per catalog capability, chosen once) and `_publish`, leaving `finalize_run` as the four-line composition.

findings.title: The catalog seam is duck-typed by hasattr/getattr while a Protocol exists that describes a different, smaller contract
findings.why: There are genuinely two implementations (`LocalCatalog`, `CatalogServiceClient`), which is precisely when `type-safety.md` says to define a Protocol — and one exists, describing a contract the code no longer uses. Because the real seam is `Any`, no checker can see that `LocalCatalog` lacks `commit`; the difference is discovered at runtime by `hasattr`, and the divergent branch it selects is one the local test suite structurally cannot reach (runtime.py:359-362 says so explicitly: "STRUCTURALLY INVISIBLE TO THE SUITE: this branch runs only when the catalog has `commit`, and `LocalCatalog` … does not"). That is how the empty-fragment 400 shipped: a code path with no type coverage and no test coverage.
findings.recommendation: Replace `CatalogClient` with the contract actually in use — `ensure`, `describe_version`, `commit`, `publish`, `register_version` — and split the optional operations into a second Protocol (`CommittingCatalog`) so `isinstance`/type narrowing replaces `hasattr`. Type `_catalog()` as the union and dispatch on the narrowed type. Then add a fake implementing the committing Protocol so the catalog branch of `finalize_run` becomes testable.

findings.title: The scope is ~45-58% prose (52% overall, measured), and the prose is PR narrative — dated measurements, named test files, and a changelog of past defects
findings.why: `code-style.md` § Comments is explicit: "The default is no comment… No metadata in comments (C1). Git owns authorship, dates, tickets, and change history", and "Don't reference the current task, fix, or callers (`# added for the X flow`, `# used by Y`) — those belong in the PR description and rot." The cost is already visible in this scope: the docstrings disagree with the code in at least two places (`StagingOverlapError` documents an isolation claim it then retracts; `emit_terminal`'s "best-effort by construction" was false until a test caught it, per the file's own note), and the module docstring for `queue.py` still asserts WORK_QUEUE semantics as a fact when the code below it exists to warn that the deployed stream may not have them. Prose at this density stops being read, and stops being maintained, which is how it starts lying.
findings.recommendation: Keep the *why* — the non-obvious constraints (ack-contract vs Lance fragment sizing, why partitioning is a column, why fragment ids collide, why chunks not units). Move the incident narrative, the dated measurements and the test-file references into the commit messages and `docs/DECISIONS.md`, which already exists and is cited. Target a comment block shorter than the code it introduces; delete every sentence whose subject is a previous version of the file.

findings.title: A boto3 client is constructed per staging call (twice per read/purge), and the S3 response bodies are never closed
findings.why: `resource-management.md` § "Always use context managers for resources needing cleanup": an unclosed `StreamingBody` holds its underlying urllib3 connection out of the pool until GC, and `discover_staged` opens one per manifest — hundreds to thousands for a real run. boto3 client construction is not cheap (session, endpoint resolution, credential chain, model loading); paying it once per staged fragment puts it directly in the ack-latency path the worker is trying to keep short, and paying it twice per read/purge is pure duplication of the same object within one call.
findings.recommendation: Cache the client at module level behind `@lru_cache` on a module-level function (not an instance method), or thread one client through `_read_all`/`_list_object_keys`/`purge_staged` from a single construction per operation. Close response bodies — `with client.get_object(...)["Body"] as body: yield body.read().decode()`.

findings.title: publish_units awaits one JetStream publish per unit and discards the PubAck, so a chunk is 1000 sequential round-trips and dedupes are reported as accepted
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-15: sequentially awaiting independent I/O. The module docstring justifies the direct NATS client partly on "batch `fetch()` — one round trip per N units instead of per unit, across millions of units", and then publishes per unit with a full round-trip each. For a million-unit run that is a million serial acks on the critical path between enumeration and any work starting. Separately, discarding `PubAck.duplicate` means the one signal that would reveal a workflow replay re-publishing a chunk is thrown away, and the activity reports the full chunk as newly queued — hiding exactly the condition the dedupe id was added to absorb.
findings.recommendation: Publish concurrently with bounded fan-out (`asyncio.gather` over slices, or `js.publish` futures) and count accepted vs duplicate from the returned `PubAck`, returning both. Log the duplicate count at INFO — it is the direct observability signal for replayed `publish_units` activities.

findings.title: InMemoryRunStore grows without bound and re-sorts the whole map on every recent() call
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-16: caches over unbounded key spaces are a finding. This is a read-side index on a long-lived pod that accepts runs indefinitely; one `RunRecord` per run is small, but the key space is unbounded and the docstring's own framing ("Losing it costs a re-read, never correctness") is the argument FOR bounding it — nothing is lost by eviction. `recent()` being O(n log n) over that unbounded set makes the polling endpoint degrade as the pod ages.
findings.recommendation: Back it with a bounded `OrderedDict` / `collections.deque` capped at a few hundred entries (or TTL-evicted), evicting oldest on insert. `recent()` then reads the tail directly instead of sorting. The `record_from_workflow_state` fallback already covers anything evicted, so bounding costs nothing.

findings.title: Generator workflows annotated as returning their final value, plus Any seams and a stale type-ignore that the QueueMessage Protocol already covers
ensure_stream treats every add_stream exception as "already exists" and logs it at DEBUG
Unreferenced helper and a legacy field still written on every manifest
The ingest write door opens completely when APP_API_TOKEN is unset — and ingest is the only governed service with no startup guard closing that path
findings.why: auth.py's own module docstring states the stakes: "with `local-dir` it was one unauthenticated request to read the ingest pod's own filesystem into a governed table, and with `s3-prefix` it is an unauthenticated writer into any project's bronze tier." A blanked/rotated-away/typo'd `APP_API_TOKEN` in a Dapr-enabled deployment silently restores exactly that, and nothing reports it — the pod comes up healthy, `/api/health` is green, and the first symptom is data. medallion's identically-shaped `authorize_produce` has the same `if not expected: return`, but medallion's producer refuses to boot in that state; ingest does not, so the dev-open path is not actually confined to dev here.
findings.recommendation: Call `assert_app_token_configured(dapr_enabled=<the same flag the other five read>)` in `create_app()` (or at the head of `_lifespan`) so the pod crash-loops rather than serving an unauthenticated write door. Keep the dev-open branch — it is a recorded decision pinned by `test_ingest_auth.py:104` — but make it unreachable once Dapr ingest is on, and add the startup-guard test.

findings.title: Blocking OIDC discovery + JWKS network IO runs inside async def — every bearer-authenticated ingest request can stall the event loop for up to 15 s
findings.why: One cold cache, one TTL expiry, or one IdP key rotation blocks the single event loop of the whole pod — every in-flight ingest POST, every status poll and `/api/health` queue behind a 15-second synchronous HTTP GET. The service already demonstrates it knows the rule (`_DaprWorkflowStarter.start` explicitly uses `to_thread` because "the client is SYNCHRONOUS gRPC, so calling it directly would block the event loop for every other request") and then does the forbidden thing one module over. In `list_ingests` the verifier is called once per record in a loop, so a cache miss lands inside an N-iteration path.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the verification in `await asyncio.to_thread(verifier.verify, raw)` (or `asyncer.asyncify`) at auth.py:151 — one line, no signature change. Longer term, give `OIDCVerifier` an async `verify` backed by the app's shared `httpx.AsyncClient` so the discovery/JWKS fetches are awaited rather than threaded.

findings.title: One router, two incompatible error contracts: four domain HTTPExceptions bypass the problem+json translator this app installs
findings.why: A generated or spec-conformant client dispatches on the numeric `code` and the `application/problem+json` media type. Half of this router's failures carry both and half carry neither, so the same client needs two parsers for one endpoint, and the `Retry-After` 503 (api.py:171) — the one failure a caller is explicitly told to retry — is the shape that lies about its own contract. This is exactly the split HOUSE-RULE-5 names for the Lance plane, and it is invisible to the suite because every API test mounts the router on a bare `FastAPI()` with no `install_problem_handlers`.
findings.recommendation: Raise `lance_namespace` typed errors instead: `InvalidInputError` for the unknown kind (api.py:130) and for `SizingRefused` (api.py:144), the not-found error for a missing run (api.py:283), and `ServiceUnavailableError` for the schedule timeout (api.py:171) — the last needs a small `Retry-After` carry-through in `install_problem_handlers` or a dedicated handler. Add a test that builds the app via `create_app()` and asserts `content-type == application/problem+json` on a 400 and a 404.

findings.title: s3-prefix builds a bare pyarrow S3FileSystem that ignores every RASK_S3_* knob — while its docstring claims it goes through the estate's provider-agnostic client
findings.why: `s3-prefix` is the plane's primary non-IIIF source and the whole reason the registry exists (`adapters.py:3-8`: it "sat written-and-unwired for months"). In-cluster it points at RustFS via `RASK_S3_ENDPOINT_URL`; this construction ignores that and resolves to real AWS unless the caller hand-types `options.endpoint` on every single request — and even then `endpoint_override` alone drops the scheme/TLS handling `objectfs.s3_filesystem` was written for (its docstring: "hardcoding `http` once silently downgraded a secured connection"). The docstring asserting the opposite is worse than silence: a reader auditing the MinIO-agnostic rule greps for the claim, finds it, and moves on.
findings.recommendation: Build the filesystem through `service_kit.lakehouse.objectfs.s3_filesystem(...)` seeded from the same env `packages/storage.client` reads (endpoint, insecure, CA bundle, region), keeping `options.endpoint` as a per-request override. Correct the docstring to name what it actually calls. Add a moto-backed adapter test that asserts the endpoint comes from `RASK_S3_ENDPOINT_URL` with no `options.endpoint`.

findings.title: GET /ingests authorizes with a loop of up to 200 sequential FGA checks instead of batch_check/list_objects
findings.why: A 200-run page is 200 serialised OpenFGA round-trips plus 200 `audit(...)` lines for one list request; at the FGA client's configured timeout the tail latency is unbounded in practice, and the audit stream is flooded with per-row `can_administer` entries that make a genuine denial unfindable. The distinct-project count is far smaller than the record count (runs cluster per project), so the useful query is one `list_objects`/`batch_check` over the distinct projects, then an in-memory filter.
findings.recommendation: Collect `{r.project for r in records}`, resolve visibility once via `fga.batch_check` (or `list_objects(relation="can_administer", type="project")`), and filter the records against that set. Emit one audit line for the list operation rather than one per row.

findings.title: The same list loop swallows an FGA/authn outage as if it were a denial — an incident renders as an empty list at DEBUG
findings.why: That exact reasoning is honoured in `_require_admin` and then discarded here by a blanket `except Exception`. With OpenFGA down, `GET /ingests` returns `200 {"runs": [], "authoritative": false}` — indistinguishable from "you own no runs" — and the only trace is a DEBUG line that is off in production. The comment justifying DEBUG is correct for a denial and wrong for the outage it also catches.
findings.recommendation: Catch the verdict types explicitly (`except (PermissionDeniedError, UnauthenticatedError): continue`) and let `ServiceUnavailableError` propagate to the problem+json handler as a 503; log any other exception at WARNING rather than swallowing it. If ING-05 is done first this collapses naturally, since the batched check has one failure point instead of N.

findings.title: No service settings model: 25 scattered os.getenv reads across 8 files, several frozen at import time, with one convention read three different ways
findings.why: There is no single place to read what this service is configured with, no validation, and no fail-fast on a malformed value — `int(os.getenv("RASK_INGEST_HTTP_ATTEMPTS", "3"))` raises `ValueError` at *import* on a typo, which surfaces as an opaque container crash rather than a config error. The import-time freeze also means the three retry knobs and the catalog delimiter cannot be moved by `kubectl set env` without a restart, while the sizing knobs next door can — an inconsistency a reader has to discover per variable. And `naming.py`'s own module docstring is a 20-line argument that "two writers of one convention will drift", written above the third copy of the delimiter.
findings.recommendation: Add `ingest/config.py` with an `IngestSettings(BaseSettings)` (`env_prefix="RASK_INGEST_"` plus explicit aliases for the shared `RASK_CATALOG_*`/`RASK_LINEAGE_*`/`RASK_S3_*` names) and an `@lru_cache get_settings()`; fold `IngestAuthSettings` in as a nested group. Convert every site above to read it, keep the delimiter in `naming.py` alone and have `catalog_service`/`lineage` import it.

findings.title: A fresh HTTP client is built for every outbound call — including one per fetched unit, the exact defect this service's own docstring warns against
findings.why: Per-unit client construction converts every fetch into a fresh TCP + TLS handshake against a source the service documents as RST-prone under load, defeating the `fetch_concurrency` ceiling `sizing.py` exists to tune. `storage.s3_client` construction is worse than a socket: botocore loads and parses its service JSON models per client, so a large `s3-prefix` run pays that cost per object.
findings.recommendation: Give `UriFetcher` its own `httpx.Client` and boto3 client, constructed once per worker and closed on teardown (it is already a class — the fields belong on it). Give `CatalogServiceClient` a single `httpx.Client` built in `__init__` and closed in a `close()`/context manager, replacing the seven `httpx.post` calls. Keep `provenance.LineageProvenanceReader` on the app's shared client via `app.state`.

findings.title: _fetch_http is a near-verbatim copy of storage.iiif.fetch_image's retry loop, assert-for-control-flow included
findings.why: Two copies of one policy that have already drifted (408/425). The `assert` is a real latent bug on both sides: under `python -O` the assertion is stripped and `raise last` executes with `last = None`, turning an exhausted-retry failure into `TypeError: exceptions must derive from BaseException` — the unit's real error is lost and the worker's failure report names the wrong thing. And the module docstring's own conclusion ("the fix is not to abstract it, it is to implement the generic policy generically") argues for a shared generic implementation, which is what tenacity is.
findings.recommendation: Replace the loop with a tenacity `@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(...), wait=wait_exponential_jitter(), retry=retry_if_exception(...))` decorator carrying the 4xx rule once, and have `storage.iiif.fetch_image` use the same decorator. If the hand-rolled loop is kept, replace `assert last is not None` with an explicit `if last is None: raise RuntimeError(...)` at both sites.

findings.title: The 202's Location header points at /v1/ingests/{run_id} — a path this service never serves under any prefix
findings.why: `Location` on a 202 is the standard handle a client follows to poll the accepted resource; here it resolves to a 404 both in-pod and through the edge. The frontend is unaffected only because it ignores the header and rebuilds the path itself — so the contract is broken for every other client and nothing notices. The suite cannot catch it: `test_ingest_api.py:78` asserts `res.headers["Location"].endswith(res.json()["run_id"])`, which any string ending in the id satisfies, and all API tests mount the router on a bare prefix-less `FastAPI()`.
findings.recommendation: Build the header from the actual mount point — `request.url_for("get_ingest", run_id=run_id)` (or `request.scope["root_path"]` + `settings.api_prefix`) — rather than a literal, and fix the three docstrings to say `/api/ingests`. Assert the header against `app.openapi()['paths']` (or simply `client.get(res.headers["Location"]).status_code == 200`) in a test that builds the app via `create_app()`.

findings.title: The OpenFGA client is built on app.state and never closed — the lifespan's cleanup block disposes only the workflow runtime
authorize_ingest is a pseudo-dependency: its Header/Depends annotations are inert because all three call sites invoke it positionally inside route bodies
findings.why: `Depends`/`Header` in a signature that is only ever called directly is decoration that reads as wiring — a maintainer adding a header (or a fourth route) has to remember to thread it through three route signatures and three call sites, and the compiler cannot help. It is also 15 lines of duplicated header plumbing across the router, and it is why the 14 auth tests had to build a surrogate app with a stub route: the real routes' authorization wiring is not addressable through `dependency_overrides`.
findings.recommendation: Split it the way medallion did: keep the pure decision function taking explicit values, and wrap it as a router-level FastAPI dependency (`Annotated[None, Depends(...)]`) that resolves the three headers itself; where the project comes from the body or the resolved record (`create_ingest`, `get_ingest`), pass it through a small dep that reads it. Drop the now-redundant header parameters from the three route signatures.

findings.title: get_auth_settings is uncached, so every request re-instantiates a BaseSettings that reads .env from disk — and then hand-patches a field from os.environ
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-9 asks for `@lru_cache get_settings`; without it every request re-opens and re-parses `.env` and re-reads the whole `LANCE_*` env surface. It also makes the settings object mutable-per-request, so the imperative `service_project` patch is a second source of truth for one value — `IngestAuthSettings()` and `get_auth_settings()` return objects that disagree, and only the latter is correct. The lifespan call at `__init__.py:146` performs the disk read inside the event loop.
findings.recommendation: Add `@lru_cache` to `get_auth_settings` and express the override declaratively — `service_project: str = Field(default="demo", validation_alias=AliasChoices("RASK_INGEST_SERVICE_PROJECT"))` — deleting the imperative patch. Fold this into the `ingest/config.py` module proposed in ING-07.

findings.title: The A8 provenance check fetches the estate's entire unbounded /runs board and linear-scans it on every status read of a completed run
findings.why: The cost of answering "does run X exist" grows with the total number of runs the estate has ever recorded — every ingest run, every mover, every train job — and it is paid on a polled endpoint, against a graph the same lineage service is concurrently writing. The 2 s timeout (provenance.py:46) means the check silently degrades to `None` ("could not ask") once the board outgrows it, so A8 stops verifying anything without ever reporting that it stopped. `get_runs` is additionally FGA-governed per run, so a run whose outputs ingest cannot `can_get_metadata` is filtered out of the board and read back as absent — i.e. reported as a provenance defect.
findings.recommendation: Ask for the one run, not the board: add/point at a `GET /runs/{run_id}` (the lineage service already has `GET /runs/{run_id}/inputs`, so the per-run path exists) and have `has_run` treat 200 as present, 404 as absent, 401/403 as `ProvenanceRefused` — the existing three-way answer, at O(1).

findings.title: The source registry stores its callables as `object` and casts them back with three `# type: ignore[assignment]`; four public functions return bare `Any`
Three dead entry points, two of them carrying docstrings that assert they are load-bearing
The queue diagnostic returns raw exception text in its response body, and the catalog's existence probe treats any exception as 'absent'
Query-parameter clamping done by hand instead of declared, and a frozen-model idiom used on a mutable model
Blocking Lance/S3 dataset resolution runs on the event loop inside async routes
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-4: pylance/lancedb/file IO are sync; calling them inside an `async def` route blocks the event loop. Worse than a single stall — the resolution is serialised behind a `threading.Lock`, so a second coroutine hitting a cold miss blocks the *whole* loop for the duration of an S3 open, freezing every other in-flight request in the pod (probes included). The sibling `def` routes in `annotations/wire.py:39`, `save.py:56`, `tags.py:93`, `versions.py:50` call the same helper correctly on the threadpool, which shows the intended shape.
findings.recommendation: Either make `assist` and `send_items` plain `def` (they already push their one genuinely-async producer call through `run_in_threadpool`, so the inversion is small), or wrap the resolution: `handle = await run_in_threadpool(dataset_handle, state, dataset)` and `await run_in_threadpool(_refuse_unknown_datasets, state, payload)`. Prefer the latter for `send_items`, which must stay `async` for its actor awaits.

findings.title: Publish saga is fire-and-forget with a module-global in-flight set — a lost task strands the project in `publishing` forever
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-15 (create_task without holding a reference — asyncio keeps only a weak reference, so a suspended task can be GC'd) and HOUSE-RULE-11 (module globals holding mutable state). The failure is not merely a lost run: if `_drive` is collected or cancelled without its `finally` completing, `_RUNNING` retains the project id, every subsequent 60 s watchdog tick logs "already running — the tick stands down" (`:283`), and `PROJECT_EDGES` (machines.py:38-39) has **no principal-fireable edge out of `PUBLISHING`** — `SYSTEM_ONLY_EVENTS` refuses `publish_succeeded`/`publish_failed` over HTTP (project_events.py:184). The project is unrecoverable without a pod restart, which is exactly the stranding the watchdog reminder exists to prevent.
findings.recommendation: Hold a strong reference (`app.state`-scoped `set[asyncio.Task]` with `task.add_done_callback(tasks.discard)`), and make `_RUNNING` an attribute of an object owned by the lifespan rather than a module global. Better: make the guard self-healing — store a monotonic start timestamp instead of a bare id and let a tick re-drive once the entry is older than one period, so a lost task costs one extra tick rather than the project.

findings.title: Per-item actor round-trips are awaited sequentially on send, publish and list — up to 2000 serialised sidecar calls in one request
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-15: independent I/O awaited sequentially. At the module's own 1000-task cap this is 2000 serialised cross-process Dapr calls inside one HTTP request; at even 20 ms each that is 40 s, past any gateway/ingress timeout. The recovery is not free: the module docstring at `:388-394` argues the seed→index order specifically to make a crash mid-send safe *because re-sending repairs it* — a timed-out send therefore requires a manual re-send, and the publish precondition reads a half-populated index until someone does. `collect()` has the same shape on the publish path, which the actor docstring (project_actor.py:8-11) explicitly says must "not be slow or flaky".
findings.recommendation: Apply the pattern already present at `project_events.py:507`: bound concurrency with `asyncio.Semaphore` and fan out with `asyncio.gather`/`TaskGroup`. Per-task the seed→send order must stay sequential, but *different* tasks are independent, so gather over items with the two calls chained inside one coroutine. Same for `saga.collect` (gather `get`+`get_draft` per task) and `projects.list_projects`.

findings.title: CORS `allow_methods` omits PUT/PATCH/DELETE while seven routes serve exactly those methods
findings.why: The shared media middleware was written for the read-plane (GET/POST only) and the annotator inherited it unchanged when it grew a write plane. Any cross-origin browser call to save a draft, patch an ontology, grant/revoke a member, adjudicate or drop a task fails at preflight. It is latent today only because the annotator zone reaches :8103 server-side through its own BFF (`frontend/microfrontends/annotator/src/routes/api/tasks/[task_id]/import/+server.ts:17`), so nothing has forced the discovery — a config that is wrong and untested is a trap for the first direct-browser consumer.
findings.recommendation: Either make `allow_methods` a `Settings` field the annotator widens, or derive it. Add a test that asserts the CORS method set is a superset of `{r.methods for r in app.routes}` — that turns the class of bug into a build failure rather than a browser console message.

findings.title: Ontology enforcement fails open on the two BULK-WRITE paths (send + import) when a stored ontology will not parse
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-5 (log-and-continue hiding real failures). The closed-set label check is the control the ontology module's own docstring says the whole redesign exists to provide ("`label=\"asdf\"` submitted and published", ontology.py:13-16). Because every model is `extra="forbid"`, an ontology written by a newer pod during a rolling upgrade fails `model_validate` on an older pod — which then treats it as "constrains nothing" and accepts arbitrary labels, at WARNING level, with a 201/200. The fail-open direction is reasoned for `assist` (never lose a prediction a human is watching) but is not defensible for the bulk `send` path, where the module's own comment at `:362-363` says "one click is five hundred rows".
findings.recommendation: Split the posture explicitly rather than by accident: keep fail-open for `assist`, and make `send_items` / `import_annotations` fail **closed** on an unparseable ontology (raise `ConflictError` naming the project and the parse error). At minimum log at ERROR and emit a counter — a governance control that turned itself off should not look like routine noise. Consider relaxing `extra="forbid"` to `extra="ignore"` on the *read* path so forward-compatible documents parse.

findings.title: Domain errors cross the actor boundary as formatted strings reconstructed by regex
findings.why: The single seam every actor call passes through reconstructs a typed domain exception from a human-readable message that `IllegalTransition.__init__` (machines.py:24) happens to format. The coupling is invisible: changing that f-string — or a `StrEnum` repr, or Dapr's envelope escaping — silently degrades every refusal to the `IllegalTransition("task", "unknown", text)` fallback at `:81`, which is what the docstring says already happened once in production (a precondition reaching the UI as a bare 500). `"IllegalTransition" not in message` is also a substring test against an arbitrary error body. There is no test for this path (`test_actor_proxy_names.py` covers name mapping only).
findings.recommendation: Carry the refusal as **data**, not as an exception: have the actor return `{"ok": False, "error": {"kind": ..., "state": ..., "event": ...}}` for a refused transition and let the proxy raise `IllegalTransition(**payload["error"])` from a structured field. If the exception path must stay, at minimum add round-trip tests over the real Dapr envelope escaping so the regex has a regression guard.

findings.title: Half the routes return bare `dict[str, Any]` — raw actor documents reach clients with no schema or filtering
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-4 / fastapi core-conventions: a return type or `response_model` is what filters fields and drives Rust-side serialization, and it is the OpenAPI contract the frontend generates against. `dict[str, Any]` documents nothing. Concretely, `fire_project_event` returns the whole project document — including `pending_publish_by`, `pending_publish_id`, `publish_error` and `publish_progress` (models.py:305-332) — to any caller holding `can_manage`, and `list_project_tasks` (`:481`) merges raw task documents carrying `transitions` and `review_notes` into an untyped envelope. Nothing declares which of those are part of the API.
findings.recommendation: Declare response models for the recurring shapes: `AnnotationProject` for the project-returning routes (already exists), a `Task` view for the task routes, and small envelopes for `send_items` / `list_project_tasks` / `list_projects`. Where the internal document is wider than the wire shape, use `response_model=` on the decorator so the filtering is real rather than implied.

findings.title: Version history opens and scans one Lance snapshot per version, up to 200 per request
findings.why: Each iteration is a fresh dataset checkout plus a filtered scan; at `limit=200` that is 200 snapshot opens and 200 scans in one request against a table that lives on S3. The annotations table gains a version on every save, so the `ds.versions()` call itself grows without bound on an actively-reviewed corpus and is fully materialised before being truncated. The catalog-mode sibling `catalog_annotation_versions` (`:97-115`) has the same per-version `count_rows` shape but at least asks the catalog for a server-side capped, descending list (`reader.versions(limit=limit)`), which is the pattern the local path is missing.
findings.recommendation: Ask Lance for the newest N versions rather than all of them, and drop the per-version row count to an opt-in query parameter — the compare-versions panel needs the timeline far more often than it needs each snapshot's cardinality. If the counts must stay, cache them by (table, version, unit) since a historical version's count is immutable.

findings.title: `project_facet` rescans every published row once per distinct task — quadratic on the publish path
findings.why: O(distinct_tasks × len(rows)). A project at the send cap (1000 tasks, project_events.py:413) whose items carry the `SendItem.prediction` cap of 200 shapes each yields up to 200k rows, so the loop performs on the order of 2×10^8 dict lookups — inside the publish saga, which the actor docstring says "must not be slow or flaky" (project_actor.py:9). The information wanted is one pass: the first row per task id.
findings.recommendation: Single pass: `first_by_task: dict[str, dict] = {}` then `for r in plan.rows: first_by_task.setdefault(r["task_id"], r)`, and derive `origins`/`datasets` from `first_by_task.values()`. Iteration order of `plan.rows` is already deterministic, so the byte-identical-replay property the docstring depends on is preserved.

findings.title: Multi-write create/send sequences have no compensation — a mid-sequence failure leaves an unusable project and relies on the caller retrying
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-7 names Dapr Workflow for durable multi-step orchestration; here the durability argument is "both halves are idempotent, so a failure here is answered by retrying the create" (`:107-109`) — which is true only if a client actually retries. If `grant_on_create` fails after the actor create and the tenant registration succeeded, the caller sees a 5xx and the estate is left with a project that exists, is listed on the tenant landing, and on which **no relation resolves for anyone** — permanently, unless the operator happens to re-POST the identical create. Nothing in the service detects or repairs that state.
findings.recommendation: Either fold the sequence into a Dapr Workflow (the sidecar is already a hard dependency for the actors) or make it self-healing: reseed ownership idempotently on read/`GET /projects/{id}` when the tuple set is empty and the caller is `created_by`, and reverse the order so the FGA grant lands before tenant registration (an unregistered-but-owned project is recoverable; an owned-by-nobody one is not).

findings.title: Actor documents grow without bound and are fully re-serialized on every event
Arrow-IPC import reads and materializes an unbounded request body
findings.why: An authenticated annotator holding `can_annotate` on any project can post an arbitrarily large body; it is buffered in memory, decoded to an Arrow table, and then converted to a Python list of dicts (typically several times the wire size). Every other bulk surface in this service is explicitly capped — `SendItemsRequest.items` at 1000 (project_events.py:138), `SendItem.prediction` at 200 (`:132`), `FireRequest.shape_ids` at 500 (tasks.py:76) — which makes the one uncapped ingress the outlier rather than a considered exemption.
findings.recommendation: Reject on `Content-Length` above a configured `ANNOTATOR_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES` before reading, and cap `table.num_rows` in `shapes_from_ipc` with a `ValidationError` naming the limit, consistent with its other refusals.

findings.title: Route prefixes are inconsistent inside one service — `/api`, `/api/jobs` and bare `/projects` / `/tasks`
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-6 (violations within a service's chosen layout). The service has no single URL namespace, so half of it is reachable through the gateway and half only by addressing :8103 directly; a consumer cannot infer the shape of one route group from another, and the inconsistency has already leaked into the frontend as a documented special case. The `api/v1/` directory name also promises a `/v1` segment that no route carries.
findings.recommendation: Pick one prefix for the whole service and mount it once in `api/v1/router.py` (`APIRouter(prefix="/api")`), leaving each endpoint router with only its resource segment. Add the resulting prefixes as gateway rows so every group is reachable the same way, and update the zone BFF to drop the special case.

findings.title: Publish transport builds a fresh httpx connection per call and retries on only one of its two paths
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-10: a client per call re-opens the pool; and the retry policy is split across two transports in one class so the create and tag halves of a single saga step behave differently under a flapping catalog. The app already owns a long-lived `httpx.Client` on `app.state.resources.http` (main.py:41), which the jobs and assist endpoints correctly reuse (`jobs.py:118`, `assist.py:378`) — the publish transport simply does not reach for it.
findings.recommendation: Give `CatalogPublisher` an injected `httpx.Client` (the lifespan-owned one, or its own built once in the publisher's constructor) and centralise the retry in one place — either tenacity around `_call`/`_create` with `retries=0` on the SDK client, or the SDK's retries with none in the app. Do not leave both configured on sibling paths.

findings.title: `@dataclass` on a value object where the house rule is Pydantic
`Any` used for collaborators that already have a declared Protocol
Throwaway class as a response stand-in, and a doubled `.json()` parse, in the publish transport
Shutdown closes resource slots the annotator never populates
Function-local stdlib imports beyond the cases the convention justifies
Member grant/revoke uses DELETE with a required request body
services/lineage/tests is absent from root testpaths — 18 tests, including two security regressions, never run
findings.why: Pytest discovery is explicit here (HOUSE-RULE-1), so a suite outside testpaths is silently inert. These two files were written as regression pins for a measured privilege-escalation (shared app token claiming `service-trainer`, `writer` on `namespace:models`) and a measured 403-on-every-honest-producer bug. A refactor of `_service_principal` or `is_external_source` that reintroduces either defect goes green in CI. That is worse than having no tests: the files' existence asserts a protection the gate does not actually enforce.
findings.recommendation: Add `"services/lineage/tests"` to `testpaths` in the root `pyproject.toml`, then run the suite and reconcile the `@pytest.mark.anyio` markers with the house `@pytest.mark.asyncio` convention. Audit the other lance-plane services for the same omission — `services/catalog`, `medallion`, `maintenance`, `viewer`, `search`, `annotator` are equally absent from that list.

findings.title: The Dapr secret store is addressed by two different env-var names — the settings one is ignored on the auth path
findings.why: Failure scenario: an operator points the estate at a differently-named store with the documented `LINEAGE_DAPR_SECRET_STORE=prod-secrets`. `apply_dapr_secrets()` (config.py:215) correctly reads `prod-secrets`, so boot succeeds and S3/DB secrets land. `_dedicated_token()` still queries the hardcoded default `lance-secrets`, gets `{}` back, returns `None` — and every request from a subject listed in `LINEAGE_PRIVILEGED_SUBJECTS` is refused with `UnauthenticatedError("...is privileged but has no dedicated credential provisioned")` (security.py:124). The deployment looks correctly configured; the privileged lane is dead.
