This also violates HOUSE-RULE-9 outright: three `os.environ` reads live outside the settings module (`APP_API_TOKEN` at security.py:106 is the third).
findings.recommendation: Delete `_dedicated_token`'s two `os.environ.get` calls and pass `settings.dapr_secret_store` / `settings.dapr_secret_key` down from `_service_principal` (which already receives `SettingsDep`). Promote `APP_API_TOKEN` to a `LineageSettings` field too, so the whole auth path reads one config object. If the two stores are genuinely meant to differ, they need two distinctly-named settings fields with that intent documented.

findings.title: repository.py is a 1382-line God module mixing a Cypher DSL, two storage surfaces, DDL bootstrap, cluster coordination and event synthesis
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-6 names 1000+ line files mixing concerns as a flag within a sanctioned layout. The concrete cost is already visible: the module needs a 30-line comment block (lines 506-519) to explain the deadlock-avoidance lock ordering inside `ingest_event`, because that invariant spans the same function as facet parsing, JSON encoding and edge linking. `backfill_write` mixing graph writes with OpenLineage envelope construction is why the spec-conformance bug at lines 1085-1096 (`eventType: RECONCILED` is not in the spec enum; facets missing `_producer`/`_schemaURL`) shipped and had to be found by validating 200 live events.
findings.recommendation: Split along the seams already visible in the file: `services/queries.py` (the constants), `services/ingest_repo.py` (the AGE write path), `services/graph_repo.py` (the AGE read path), `services/feed_repo.py` (the two `public.*` relational tables), `services/bootstrap.py` (the `ensure_*` DDL, called once from the lifespan), and move the synthetic-event construction in `backfill_write` into `service_kit.openlineage` next to `custom_facet`/`run_id_for`. Then drop `C901` and `E501` from the `services/lineage/**` per-file-ignores so the gate holds the new shape.

findings.title: Every list/browse read is an unbounded fetch-all with no server-side LIMIT, on endpoints documented as polled every 2s
findings.why: `:Run` nodes grow without bound by default — `run_retention_days: int = Field(default=0, ...)` (config.py:158) means retention is OFF unless opted in, and the docstring calls 0 "the dev/demo default". So `/runs` (2s poll) reads every run ever ingested, and `/graph` reads every WROTE edge ever created, on every tick. The only bound is the 30s `statement_timeout` (config.py:34), which converts steady growth into an abrupt, total failure of the board rather than a degradation. The comments justify the design as "the graph's node count is modest" (repository.py:115) — true of `:Dataset`, false of `:Run`, and `_ESTATE_WRITES` scales with `:Run`.
findings.recommendation: Push `LIMIT` + ordering into the Cypher for `_LIST_RUNS`, `_PRODUCERS` and `_ESTATE_WRITES` and make the endpoint limit the query parameter rather than a post-fetch slice; aggregate `_ESTATE_WRITES` in the graph (`collect(DISTINCT w.version)`) instead of returning one row per edge and folding in `_fold_writes`. Default `/events` to `summary=True` on the poll path, or drop `_EVENTS_FETCH` to a multiple of `limit` rather than a flat 2000. Consider making `run_retention_days` non-zero by default now that pruning is batched and lock-guarded.

findings.title: Uncached blocking secret-store fetch with a ~2-minute retry budget runs on every privileged-service request
findings.why: `authenticate` is a plain `def`, so FastAPI dispatches it to Starlette's threadpool (default 40 workers) — the event loop is safe, which is why this is not HIGH. But each privileged-subject request costs a full HTTP round-trip to the sidecar's secret store before the credential comparison, and if the sidecar is slow or the store is reseeding, each in-flight request pins a threadpool worker for up to two minutes while tenacity retries. Forty concurrent requests exhaust the pool and stall every synchronous route in the app. The Ray TRAIN job is documented (security.py:53-54) as POSTing every RunEvent through this door, so the request rate is per-event, not per-session.
findings.recommendation: Cache the fetched bundle behind a TTL (or fetch it once in the lifespan alongside `apply_dapr_secrets` and stash it on `app.state`) so the store is consulted at boot and on refresh, not per request. If a per-request read is genuinely required, pass a much tighter budget — `retries=1, timeout=1.0` — since a request-path secret lookup must fail fast, and the boot-time retry schedule exists for a different problem.

findings.title: prune_runs' batch size is duplicated as a Python constant and a literal baked into the Cypher — a change to one silently under-prunes
Domain values cross the models→repository boundary as untyped dicts and positional tuples while typed Pydantic twins exist on the read path
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-2/3: structured values should be Pydantic. The same schema field is a validated model when read and a bare `dict[str, str]` when written, so the two representations can drift and only the read side would notice. The dict-key contract is enforced nowhere — `edge["masking"]` is a `KeyError` at write time if `column_edges` ever stops emitting it, inside a transaction inside a Dapr subscriber whose failure mode is infinite redelivery. The positional `r[0]`…`r[11]` coupling is worse: reordering a `RETURN` clause or editing the separate `columns=N` argument produces silently wrong data with no type error and no runtime error — `producers()` would just start reporting the wrong author or version.
findings.recommendation: Give `models.py` real nested Pydantic models for the four facet payloads (`SchemaField` is already the right shape — reuse it instead of `dict[str, str]`; add `ColumnEdgeFacet`, `OutputStatistics`, `QualityAssertion`) and have the repository consume attributes. For the row unpacking, replace positional indexing with a small per-query row model (`RowT.model_validate(dict(zip(COLUMNS, row)))`) or at minimum derive `columns=` from a named tuple of column names declared beside each query constant, so the count and the ordering cannot diverge.

findings.title: Route topology is decided at import time by four settings-conditional module-level gates, none drivable from a test
findings.why: Which routes exist — including two of the three ingest paths and the cron sweep — is frozen when the module is first imported, against an `lru_cache`d settings object. A test cannot build a second app with different settings without clearing the cache and reloading the module, which is exactly why `mount_reconcile_cron` had to be extracted as a named function with a docstring explaining that "the audit's gap was the route being tested only on a synthetic app" (main.py:174-176). That fix addresses one of four such gates; the demo mount, the docs gate and the Dapr subscription have the same shape and no equivalent seam. Module-level `app` is expected in layout (b), but settings-conditional wiring at import is not.
findings.recommendation: Extract `def create_app(settings: LineageSettings | None = None) -> FastAPI` that performs all conditional wiring from its argument, and keep `app = create_app()` at module level for `uvicorn lineage.main:app`. `register_dapr(app, settings)` should take settings rather than calling `get_settings()` itself. That makes all four gates drivable from a test without cache surgery.

findings.title: The AGE pool leaks if any of the seven lifespan bootstrap steps fails after pool.open()
The cron sweep is a 114-line function, and reconcile_all serially awaits three independent round-trips per dataset
findings.why: Two rules at once. The function-shape rule ("20–50 lines, one purpose") — the five WARN blocks are a copy-paste family that should be a table of `(predicate, message, extractor)` driven by one loop, and the log-extra/response duplication means a new axis must be added in three places. And HOUSE-RULE-15 — `source_uri`, `dropped_at` and `latest_write_version` for a given dataset are independent reads that could be one `asyncio.gather`, and datasets are independent of each other; instead an N-dataset estate costs at least 3N sequential AGE round-trips with 3N pool checkout/checkin cycles against a pool of `max_size=8`, all inside the cluster-wide advisory lock that blocks every other replica's sweep.
findings.recommendation: Extract the report assembly into a `SweepReport(BaseModel)` built once and used for both the log and the response, and drive the five WARN blocks from a declarative list. In `reconcile_all`, gather the three per-dataset repository reads, and bound-concurrently process datasets (`asyncio.Semaphore` + `TaskGroup`) rather than strictly serially — or better, add a single repository method that returns `(name, source_uri, last_success_op, latest_version)` for all datasets in one Cypher statement, which removes the N-fan-out entirely.

findings.title: Three un-logged `except Exception` swallows in demo.py beside an unused logger, and a BaseException catch that misreports MemoryError as an unreadable dataset
findings.why: HOUSE-RULE-5 names log-and-continue that hides real failures; these do not even log. The demo peek reads real medallion datasets with the service's root S3 credentials, so a misconfigured endpoint or expired key is indistinguishable from "the dataset doesn't exist yet" — and the operator's only signal, a `log` object, was imported and abandoned. The empty-schema case is worse because line 115 caches the failure as a valid immutable manifest entry, so a transient read error becomes a permanently-empty schema for that version. In `_swallow_dataset_error`, the `BaseException` catch is well-argued for pyo3's `PanicException`, but its allowlist omits `MemoryError` — a genuine OOM on a large dataset open is silently reclassified as "dataset unreadable", and the reconcile sweep reports `missing_on_storage` for a dataset that is fine.
findings.recommendation: Log every swallow in demo.py at WARNING with the URI and `exc_info=True` (the logger is already there), and do not cache a failed schema read as an empty one — leave the entry absent so the next tick retries. Narrow `_swallow_dataset_error` to re-raise anything that is not an `Exception` *except* the specific pyo3 panic type, or at minimum add `MemoryError` to the re-raise list.

findings.title: An unused module constant, and a 45-line 'consumer side' of the run hierarchy that no production code reads
A loop of sequential single check() calls where the module's own batch_check filter is available, and a duplicate-laden batch payload
Only one of eight routers under api/v1/endpoints/ carries a version prefix, producing a double-/api path for ingest
Module-level mutable caches in the demo endpoint, with a test-only reset seam instead of app.state
Generic return widened to Any internally, bare list defaults on two Pydantic fields, and unannotated conn params
The publication cascade head puts the project-QUALIFIED NAMESPACE on the trigger's `project` field, so every real publication is DROPped by the mover
findings.why: This head exists specifically to fix defect B8 ("the cascade moves no data"). As wired it reproduces B8 through a different door: every publication of an ingest-written table is DROPped with a FAIL run, or — where the registry happens to resolve — emits double-qualified lineage identities (`bind86-bronze-bronze$pages`) that name a dataset nothing else in the estate uses. It is the exact drift `ingest/naming.py`'s own docstring warns about, on the one side that module did not reach.
findings.recommendation: Derive the project from the namespace rather than equating them: strip the tier suffix (`namespace.removesuffix(f"-{settings.bronze_namespace}")`, empty result → single-tenant) or, better, have the catalog carry the resolved `project` explicitly in `extra` the way it already carries `location`/`from_version`, and read it there. Then extend `tests/unit/test_publication_trigger.py` with the real id shape (`table:bind86-bronze$pages` → `project == "bind86"`), asserting against `ingest.naming.bronze_namespace_for` so the two sides cannot drift again.

findings.title: The in-process HTR lane holds the Dapr ack — and a process-wide asyncio.Lock — across the entire multi-page GPU transcription
findings.why: ackWait expires long before the stage returns, so the sidecar redelivers; each redelivery enters `handle_stage`, blocks on `_write_lock`, and pins a Starlette threadpool worker (default 40) while waiting. When the lock finally releases the redelivery re-reads every page and re-runs every GPU inference from scratch — N× the compute cost per redelivery, up to `maxDeliver`, then the DLQ. The A13 rework removed exactly this shape from the Ray stage path but left it on the in-process/HTR path, which `transform.py:249-254` dispatches to FIRST, ahead of the Ray branch.
findings.recommendation: Give the HTR lane the same submit-and-ack shape the Ray stage path already has: dispatch the transcription as a job (or an internal durable task) and return SUCCESS immediately, letting the registered commit + publication event wake the next tier. Until P7b lands, at minimum bound the handler (`asyncio.timeout` well inside ackWait, returning RETRY) and make `_write_lock` acquisition non-blocking (`if _write_lock.locked(): return _RETRY`) so redeliveries do not queue up holding workers.

findings.title: The S3 secret key and the estate's APP_API_TOKEN are shipped into the Ray Jobs `runtime_env`, which the Jobs API echoes back to any reader
findings.why: House rule 7 makes the Dapr/OpenBao secret store the SOLE source and fail-closed; that posture is undone at the last hop by copying the plaintext secret into a REST body that the Ray dashboard/Jobs API renders back to anyone who can `GET /api/jobs/<id>` (the same dashboard `services/compute` proxies at `/api/ray/*`). `APP_API_TOKEN` is the estate-wide service credential guarding every `require_dapr_token` route — a read of one job's runtime_env yields the key to the whole cascade, `/lineage-events` included.
findings.recommendation: Stop transporting credentials through `runtime_env`. Mount the S3 credentials and the lineage service token onto the Ray worker pods (k8s Secret / the same OpenBao-backed Dapr secret component the fleet already uses) and pass only the non-secret pointers (`FROM_URI`, `TO_URI`, `STAGE`, `MODEL`, `REGISTRY_URI`, OTEL config) in `runtime_env`. If the KubeRay merge is the intended point for this, gate the current path behind an explicit dev-only flag so a production render cannot take it.

findings.title: `handle_stage` is a 473-line God function that is the entire module — lane routing, tenant resolution, authz, compute dispatch, lineage, quality gate and four failure taxonomies in one body
findings.why: Every rule in the design-patterns reference is breached at once: functions of 20-50 lines, one reason to change, guard clauses over pyramids. Concretely it is why MED-005 (four copies of the FAIL block) and MED-001 (the project semantics buried at :126-146, far from the head that produces them) both exist — no reviewer can hold the whole contract in view, and the four exception paths have already drifted apart in what they record (one increments `record_quality_blocked`, three do not).
findings.recommendation: Split along the seams the code already marks with its own numbered comments: `_discriminate_lane(data, settings) -> str | None`, `_resolve_roots(settings, project) -> tuple[str, str]`, `_authorize(fga_client, settings, to_namespace) -> Verdict`, `_run_compute(...) -> WriteResult | None`, `_emit_complete(...)`, `_trigger_next(...)`, and one `_emit_fail(...)` (see MED-005). `handle_stage` then reads as ~40 lines of guard clauses and calls, and each piece becomes independently testable — today the only entry point is the full handler.

findings.title: The "build a FAIL RunEvent and publish it through the outbox" block is copy-pasted four times inside `handle_stage`
findings.why: Same knowledge (how the medallion records a failed run) expressed in four places — the DRY case the reference calls out as "unify". The copies have already diverged in ways that read as accidental rather than deliberate: only the `UnderivableMediaError` copy is preceded by `record_quality_blocked(transition)`; the outbox comment justifying the staging is present on two copies and absent on the other two.
findings.recommendation: Extract one `async def _emit_fail(dapr, settings, *, from_ref, to_ref, token, project, reason: str) -> None` holding the `suppress(Exception)` + build + outbox publish, and call it from all four sites. That is a mechanical change and it makes the metric/log asymmetry a deliberate argument rather than an accident of copying.

findings.title: Deterministic HTR page failures route to RETRY, re-running every GPU transcription in the batch — the sibling media lane already establishes the DROP contract for exactly this case
findings.why: A NULL payload, a misconfigured `htrflow_url`, or a `to_uri` outside the catalog root will fail identically on every redelivery. Each attempt re-transcribes the whole volume against a GPU endpoint budgeted at 600 s/page before hitting the same row, so one poison page burns `maxDeliver` × N page-inferences before parking. The `RegisterError` docstring acknowledges the re-run cost for a *catalog outage* (transient, correctly RETRY) but the same channel silently carries the deterministic cases too.
findings.recommendation: Classify at the seam: raise `UnderivableMediaError` (or a sibling `PermanentStageError`) for a NULL payload, a non-XML 200, an unset endpoint, and a location outside the catalog root, and let the existing `except UnderivableMediaError` DROP path record the FAIL run. Keep only genuinely transient failures (connection errors, 5xx, catalog unreachable) on the RETRY path.

findings.title: The publication trigger's `from_version`/`to_version` range is published but never read — the mover still full-overwrites the tier, so the delta contract the head exists for is unimplemented
findings.why: The head's stated justification (D-R3: "it names a table, not a delta") is not actually delivered — the mover rescans and rewrites the whole tier on every publication, which is the cost the range was introduced to avoid, and a second publication of the same table re-does all the work. The docstring asserts behaviour the code does not have, so a future reader (or a consumer relying on `_row_created_at_version > from AND <= to` semantics) is misled.
findings.recommendation: Either consume it — thread `from_version`/`to_version` into `read_upstream`/`transform_stage` as a scan predicate and switch the write to append for a delta — or delete the two fields and correct the module docstring to say the trigger is a whole-table wake-up. Leaving a documented-but-unread field is the worse of the three.

findings.title: Every outbound HTTP call builds its own httpx client — one connection pool opened and torn down per Ray submit, per catalog register, and per transcribed page
findings.why: House rule 10 and the anti-pattern table both name this: a per-call `AsyncClient` re-opens the connection pool every time (~10× slowdown, and against a TLS endpoint a full handshake per page). It also scatters the timeout/retry posture — `htr_register` hardcodes `timeout_seconds: float = 30.0` as a function default rather than reading a setting, so the catalog timeout is invisible to config.
findings.recommendation: Build one `httpx.AsyncClient` (and, for the threadpool-resident sync lanes, one `httpx.Client`) in each app's lifespan, stash on `app.state`, and inject via a small `HttpDep`/parameter. Pass the client down into `transcribe_page` / `register_gold_table` instead of a `base_url`. Move `htr_register`'s 30 s default onto `MedallionSettings` beside `htrflow_timeout_seconds`.

findings.title: `APP_API_TOKEN` is read raw from `os.environ` in two unrelated modules instead of the typed settings surface (the other 11 reads are OTel env passthrough into a child job)
The service-token comparison (env read + dev-open + compare_digest) has a second home in `authorize_produce`, though the dual-auth fall-through means the shared dependency cannot be called directly
The medallion writes OpenFGA tuples directly from a message handler — a second tuple-write path outside the catalog's `seed_ownership`
findings.why: House rule 12 asks for one tuple-write path. Beyond the policy concern, this one hardcodes `$` inside an f-string while `MedallionSettings.delimiter` (config.py:187) exists precisely because "a mismatch addresses a DIFFERENT table rather than failing" — so a non-default delimiter deployment writes a parent link onto a table id nobody queries, and the comment's stated consequence ("the published model is INVISIBLE in /runs, /datasets/*, /graph") returns silently.
findings.recommendation: Move the parent-link seeding behind the catalog's own registration/ownership door — the trainer job already registers its output, so `seed_ownership` is the natural home — or, if it must stay here, at minimum use `settings.delimiter` and `fga.canonical_object_id` instead of an inline `$`, and hoist the `ClientTuple` import to module scope.

findings.title: `htr_stage` imports four private names out of `compute`, coupling the HTR lane to the generic compute's internals
findings.why: The code-style reference is explicit: a private name used across a module boundary means either it should be public or the caller shouldn't reach in. Here it is the former — the R26 provenance-column mechanics (`lineage` name, the JSONB column builder, the JSON scalar index) are a shared contract every lane must honour, not compute's implementation detail. As written, renaming `_index_lineage` breaks the HTR lane with no signal, and `_STAGE_COLUMN` is already a second copy that can drift.
findings.recommendation: Promote the shared write contract into a public seam — e.g. a `medallion/services/lance_write.py` (or public names on `compute`) exporting `LINEAGE_COLUMN`, `STAGE_COLUMN`, `lineage_column()`, `index_lineage()`, `write_stage_table()` — and have both `compute.transform_stage` and `htr_stage.transcribe_stage` call it. That also removes the duplicated `write_dataset` flag block.

findings.title: Two handler seams are typed `Any` with an ANN401 suppression while every sibling handler is concretely typed
Both app entrypoints read settings and configure logging at import time
Unreachable return, a stale line reference, a truncated docstring — plus one inline comment (not a docstring) whose open-count claim is contradicted
`record_quality_blocked` is incremented for an undecodable-media failure that ran no quality assertion
Object-browser routes are `async def` but run blocking boto3 and a blocking Dapr secret fetch on the event loop
findings.why: Every S3 list/HEAD/GET and every cold secret lookup stalls the whole viewer process — all other in-flight requests, including `/livez`/`/readyz`, block behind one slow bucket listing or one unseeded secret store. The gate (`await checker(...)`) is what forced these functions to become coroutines; the body was never moved off the loop, and the docstring was never updated, so the file now documents the opposite of what it does.
findings.recommendation: Split the awaited authorization from the blocking body: keep `async def` for the `await _require_browse(...)` prologue and push everything from `_client_for(...)` onward through `fastapi.concurrency.run_in_threadpool` (the pattern `pages.py:_authorized_dataset` already uses), then correct the module docstring. Same treatment for `_creds`.

findings.title: Dataset enumeration routes are `async def` and open Lance/S3 (under a threading.Lock) inline on the event loop
findings.why: Worse than plain blocking IO: because `registry.get` holds a `threading.Lock`, the event loop can end up spinning on a lock owned by a threadpool worker that is mid-S3-open, so the entire process serializes behind one cold dataset. This is the first call every zone makes on page load, so the stall is on the hottest path. The sibling `voice.py:141` and `pages.py:137` already document and apply the correct `run_in_threadpool` treatment for exactly this call.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the registry work: `datasets = await run_in_threadpool(_collect_summaries, state)` and `handle = await run_in_threadpool(dataset_handle, state, dataset_id)`, leaving only the `await checker(...)` calls on the loop. Also hoist the per-dataset `registry.get` out of `_may_see` so the descriptor is read once, not twice.

findings.title: 25 of the viewer's 32 routes serve corpus content with no authn and no FGA gate, including every media-byte route
findings.why: The service's own `security.py` docstring is explicit that the untrusted-network posture "stops being defensible the moment more than one person can reach the zone," and that a corpus LIST alone is sensitive. Yet the list is gated while the bytes, the transcripts, the entity graph and the atlas selection rows behind it are not — anyone who can reach `:8101` (or `/api/explorer/*` through the gateway) reads every corpus in full. A gate applied to the index but not the content is not a partial control; it is a control that can be bypassed by guessing one `doc_id`.
findings.recommendation: Decide and apply one stance per route family. At minimum, put the byte-serving routes (`/api/media`, `/api/thumbnail`, `/api/chunk-frame`, `/api/media-clip`) behind `READ_DATA` on `corpus_object(settings, dataset_id, row_table)` and the content-listing routes (transcripts, atlas chunks, graph, voice, documents) behind `READ_METADATA`, reusing the existing `CheckerDep`/`CurrentSubject` deps — applied at the `APIRouter(dependencies=[...])` level so a new route cannot be added ungated. `POST /api/graph/cypher` needs a stronger gate than the read routes, or removal from the deployed surface.

findings.title: Search result-cache key omits `spec.table`, so two different searchable tables of one corpus serve each other's hits
findings.why: The module's own docstring says "Miss one and a stale result is served, so the payload is exhaustive." One is missed. `GET /api/search?q=x&table=pages` then `GET /api/search?q=x&table=lines` against the same corpus produce identical cache keys, so the second request returns the first table's rows — with `_table` stamped as the first table, so the frontend renders them as if they were correct. Secondarily, `version_signature` only versions the default search's tables, so a write to a non-default searchable table never invalidates anything. `search_cache_size` defaults to 256 (media/config.py:47), i.e. this is on by default.
findings.recommendation: Add `"table": spec.table` to the `query_hash` payload, and make `_search_tables` resolve through `declared.search_named(spec.table)` so the version signature covers the tables actually read. Add a unit test asserting two specs differing only in `table` produce different keys — `tests/unit/test_search_table_selector.py` already exercises the selector and is the natural home.

findings.title: `/api/page` and `/api/pages` materialize every page blob in the dataset to serve one image or one metadata page
findings.why: The route's docstring correctly warns that inlining bytes into the listing "would move hundreds of megabytes to render a contact sheet" — and then the single-page route does exactly that per request. A contact sheet of 100 thumbnails issues 100 requests, each reading the entire volume: memory and S3 egress scale as O(pages²). This is the primary read path of the document viewer.
findings.recommendation: Push the predicate down: `read_aligned_table(ds, columns=[*_PAGE_COLUMNS, "payload"], filter=f"id = {page_id}")` for the single-page route, and read only `_PAGE_COLUMNS` plus a cheap null-probe (not the blob) with `limit=limit` for the listing — `has_image`/`size` can come from a blob-description read rather than the payload itself.

findings.title: Broad `except Exception` re-raised as `ValidationError` turns infrastructure faults into HTTP 400 client errors
findings.why: `except Exception` here catches an unreachable S3 endpoint, an expired credential, a corrupt Lance manifest and an OOM identically with a genuinely malformed query, and reports all of them as "you sent a bad request". A 400 tells the caller to fix their input and tells the operator nothing is wrong on the server; it also excludes the failure from any 5xx-based SLO or alert. Only `_search_hybrid`/`_search_fts` have a plausible client-error cause (a bad `where` or an unindexed column) — and even those cannot be distinguished from an outage by this handler.
findings.recommendation: Narrow the catch to the exceptions that genuinely indicate caller input (Lance/DataFusion plan or parse errors, `ValueError`) and let everything else propagate to the global handler as a 5xx. Where the underlying library does not separate them, at least classify on the message the way `target.py:137-141` already does (`if "not found" in msg ... else raise`).

findings.title: Five silent swallows in the search path hide real failures as empty results (three of the nine cited sites do log)
findings.why: Each of these converts a diagnosable failure into a plausible-looking empty or partial answer. A wrong-dimension query vector, a dropped S3 connection and "the index hasn't been built yet" all produce the same zero-result page, and `_search_all`'s FTS swallow leaves no trace anywhere. The `version_signature` case is worse than silent: a table that intermittently fails to open pins its cache entry for the process lifetime, serving stale hits after writes land.
findings.recommendation: Log every swallow at WARNING with `exc_info=True` (the two sites in `_search_all` and `_ranked_or_fallback` are the urgent ones), and narrow each to the exception that actually means "not built yet". For `version_signature`, use a value that cannot collide across attempts (e.g. a monotonic counter or `time.time_ns()`) so an unreadable table forces a miss rather than a permanent hit.

findings.title: The Cypher engine cache is a module-level mutable global holding hundreds of MB, and its lock serializes every graph request across all datasets
findings.why: Two problems. (1) Module-global mutable state breaks the test/composition seam the codebase deliberately built — `create_viewer_app` (main.py:115) can construct several apps over different `AppState`s, and they all share this dict and its `_CACHE_MAX=2` budget; nothing releases the ~370 MB engines when an app is torn down. (2) The lock is global, not per key: a cold build for dataset A holds it for ~20 s, so every `/api/graph/*` request for dataset B — including the cheap `GET /status` — blocks in the threadpool for that whole window, and with only 40 threadpool workers a handful of graph requests can starve every other sync route in the process.
findings.recommendation: Move the cache onto `AppState` beside `points_cache`/`search_cache` and key the lock per cache key (a `dict[key, Lock]` or a `Future`-per-key single-flight) so a build for one dataset does not block reads of another.

findings.title: `/api/media-clip` hands a `Host`-header-derived URL to ffmpeg — server-side request forgery
findings.why: A request with `Host: internal-metadata-service.local` makes the viewer's ffmpeg fetch that host over the pod network and transcode whatever it returns into an MP4 the caller then downloads — a read primitive against anything the pod can reach, from an unauthenticated route (see VS-03). The 120 s ffmpeg timeout also makes it a cheap resource-exhaustion lever.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive the loopback origin from the request. Build it from configuration (a `Settings` field defaulting to `http://127.0.0.1:{service_port}`), or better, bypass HTTP entirely and read the blob range directly — `stream_blob_range` is already in this module and ffmpeg can consume a pipe.

findings.title: Unsanitized S3 object key interpolated into the `Content-Disposition` header
findings.why: A key containing a double quote breaks out of the quoted `filename=` and lets the caller append arbitrary `Content-Disposition` parameters; a non-ASCII key produces a header value that is not latin-1 encodable and will raise at the ASGI layer rather than returning the file. The file-handling reference is explicit: "Anything in `filename=` that originated from user input must be sanitized — both for the path on disk and for the `Content-Disposition` header."
findings.recommendation: Apply the reference's `sanitize_filename` (strip `/\\\x00:<>"|?*` and leading/trailing dots-and-spaces) and emit both forms for non-ASCII: `filename="<sanitized>"; filename*=UTF-8''<urllib.parse.quote(name)>`.

findings.title: `_creds`' documented fail-closed handler is unreachable, so a down secret store reports "the secret is empty"
findings.why: The posture is still fail-closed (correct), but the diagnosis is inverted: an unreachable Dapr sidecar, a missing secret, and a genuinely malformed secret all report "secret 'X' exists but carries no access_key/secret_key pair", sending the operator to inspect a secret that may not be the problem at all. The dead `except` also means the `{exc}` detail the docstring promises never reaches anyone. Note the docstring's `lru_cache` reasoning ("Only SUCCESSFUL lookups cache — `lru_cache` never stores a raised exception") still holds only because the raise happens after the call, which is accidental rather than designed.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish the two states — have `_creds` treat an empty dict as "unreadable" with its own message, or (better) give `fetch_dapr_secret` a `raise_on_failure=True` mode so fail-closed callers get the real cause and the existing handler becomes live. Delete whichever branch ends up unreachable.

findings.title: `_resolve` builds a new `httpx.Client` per catalog call while a pooled client sits on `app.state`
findings.why: Every `/api/pages` and `/api/page` request opens a fresh connection pool, does a TCP+TLS handshake to the catalog, and tears it down — the ~10x cost the reference calls out — and this is on the per-image path, so a contact sheet of 100 pages performs 100 handshakes. `state.http` exists precisely to avoid that.
findings.recommendation: Take the client from `state.http` (already available via `StateDep` on both routes) and pass `timeout=30.0` per call. Keep the `httpx.RequestError` mapping.

findings.title: The search service has no authn/authz at all yet accepts a raw SQL `where` expression ANDed into every query
findings.why: A caller who can reach `:8102` (or `/api/explorer/search` through the gateway) can run arbitrary DataFusion predicates over every corpus. Even without a mutation path, boolean predicates are a byte-at-a-time exfiltration oracle for columns the hit projection deliberately excludes, and an expensive predicate with `prefilter=true` is a cheap denial-of-service against the shared Lance/S3 path. The viewer went through exactly this reasoning for its own list endpoint (`viewer/api/security.py:3-8`); search did not.
findings.recommendation: Give search the same `make_auth_deps` wiring the viewer uses (`GovernedAuthSettings` mixin + `CheckerDep`/`CurrentSubject`), gated on `can_read_data` for the resolved corpus table. Independently, either bound `where` to a parsed allowlist of `filterable` columns and comparison operators, or gate it behind a separate, more privileged relation — an untrusted raw predicate should not be reachable by the same caller who can run a plain query.

findings.title: Rerank scores are silently misaligned with candidates when the server returns a short or sparse result list
findings.why: `RerankResponse` is declared to ignore extras and carries no length invariant, and the comment "may arrive unordered" shows sparse/reordered replies were anticipated. If the vLLM server truncates (a token-budget drop on a long document, a partial failure) every subsequent hit is scored by the wrong document, and `strict=False` then silently drops the tail of `head` from the result list rather than raising. The output still looks like a ranked list, so nothing surfaces.
findings.recommendation: Build the score list positionally from the indices — `scores = [0.0] * len(candidates); for item in results: scores[item.index] = item.relevance_score` — and raise if `len(results) != len(candidates)` or an index is out of range. Change the `zip` in `rerank_by_text` to `strict=True` so a future mismatch fails loudly.

findings.title: `download_object` buffers whole objects in memory on a premise the store registry no longer guarantees
findings.why: The size assumption the design rests on was deleted when the bucket list became configuration. A deployment registering a warehouse or observability store (both are in `DEFAULT_STORES`) exposes multi-GB objects to a route that will `read()` them whole — with concurrent requests each holding a full copy, this is an OOM on an authenticated but not resource-bounded endpoint. The stale justification is what makes it invisible.
findings.recommendation: Stream via `StreamingResponse` over `resp["Body"].iter_chunks()` (keeping the client alive for the generator's lifetime), or at minimum consult `ContentLength` from a HEAD first and refuse above a configured cap with a 413. Update the docstring so it no longer asserts a two-bucket estate.

findings.title: Voice similarity issues one Lance scan per hit (N+1) and a fresh ThreadPoolExecutor per encoder call
findings.why: The N+1 is 100 sequential filtered scans of the row table for one `/api/voice/similar` request, occupying a threadpool worker for the whole duration — the sibling paths in the same file (`_attach_captions`, `_attach_speaker_clusters`, and `postprocess.attach_captions`) all already do the batched `doc IN (...)` scan and document why ("~2.4x faster, verified"). The per-call executor adds 32 thread creations and joins to every embedding request on the search hot path.
findings.recommendation: Replace the per-turn loop with one `isin(doc_key, docs)` scan over the distinct `doc_id`s plus a Python-side max-overlap pick, mirroring `_attach_captions`. Hoist the `ThreadPoolExecutor` to `VLLMTransport.__init__` and shut it down in the existing `close()` (which the lifespan already calls).

findings.title: Neither service is in `testpaths` and neither ships tests; the retrieval core and every pure helper are uncovered
findings.why: The uncovered set is exactly where the defects in this report live: `parse_range` (media.py:78-104) is a pure function encoding RFC 9110 §14.2's three-way sentinel with no test; `result_cache.query_hash` carries VS-04's collision with no test; `run_search` (423 lines, every search request) has none; `_enforce_limit` (graph.py:128-141) exists because the previous cap was bypassable and has no regression test. `service_kit/governed/deps.py:26-34` documents that a gated viewer route shipped broken for weeks because the authz tests over-stubbed the dependency — the same three viewer authz suites still stub `CheckerDep.__metadata__[0].dependency`.
findings.recommendation: Add `services/viewer/tests` and `services/search/tests` to `testpaths` and seed them with unit tests for the pure helpers first — `parse_range`, `query_hash`/`cache_key`, `_enforce_limit`, `key_predicate`/`drop_seed`, `build_where_clause`, `frames_to_row_hits` — none of which need Lance or a running service.

findings.title: Ten routes return bare `dict[str, Any]` / `list[dict[str, Any]]`, losing response filtering and the OpenAPI contract
findings.why: The reference is explicit that "return types or response models are what filter data to prevent sensitive-field exposure, and Pydantic uses them to serialize on the Rust side." With `dict[str, Any]` the rows go out exactly as Lance produced them: a descriptor gaining a column, or a `payload_columns` derivation widening, ships new fields to the browser with nothing to notice — the same class of leak `_PAGE_COLUMNS` (pages.py:39-41) was made explicit to prevent. It also means the search hit shape, the frontend's core contract, is undocumented in OpenAPI.
findings.recommendation: Define `Hit`/`AtlasStatus`/`DocTranscript`/`DocumentsPage` models in `service_kit.schemas` beside the ones already there and annotate the routes. Where the row shape is genuinely dataset-dependent, an explicit `dict[str, Any]` field on a wrapper model still pins the envelope.

findings.title: Encoder construction picks its kwargs by runtime signature introspection, to accommodate test doubles
findings.why: Production wiring is shaped by test doubles, and it fails open: if `VLLMEmbeddingClient` is ever renamed to take `url=` instead of `embed_url=`, `_construct` silently drops the argument and builds a client pointing at a default — no `TypeError`, no log, just an embedder talking to the wrong server. It also defeats `ty`: nothing type-checks the call. FastAPI already provides the seam this works around — `app.dependency_overrides[get_embedder]` (the module's own docstring at `api/dependencies.py:8-9` says tests can override there).
findings.recommendation: Delete `_construct` and call the constructors directly with their real keywords; have tests override `get_embedder`/`get_reranker` through `app.dependency_overrides`, or inject a fake by assigning `state.embedder` before the request.

findings.title: `parse_range` returns a three-way `tuple | str-sentinel | None` that the caller decodes with a rebound flag variable
Eleven route params use bare defaults instead of the `DatasetParam`/`Query(...)` aliases the same package defines
Store-name/bucket-name confusion makes the object browser's 404 name the wrong thing
Legacy `TypeVar` instead of PEP 695 type parameters, and a shadowed function parameter
`os.getenv` read for the secret-store name outside the settings module, and a private constant imported across modules
The documented compact→cleanup→optimize order invariant is not the order the code runs (two docstrings assert a sequence the implementation contradicts)
findings.why: This is the single invariant the service's whole existence is justified by ("the order is the reason these live in one service"), stated as FIXED and load-bearing in two places, and both statements are false about the shipped code. The stated rationale is also internally incoherent — it claims cleanup follows compaction and then that index optimization "must follow that", i.e. follow cleanup, which is the code's order but not the sentence's. Anyone reasoning about GC safety, step opt-outs (`cleanup_enabled` / `optimize_indices_enabled`), or a future reorder will reason from a docstring that lies. writing-python/code-style#comments: "a docstring that lies about behavior is worse than no docstring".
findings.recommendation: Decide which order is correct and make code and docs agree in one commit. If the code is right (compact → optimize_indices → cleanup, which lets the tick also GC the version the index-optimize commit created), fix the three docstrings and state the real reason. If the docstring is right, move the `cleanup_old_versions` / `enable_auto_cleanup` block above the `optimize_indices` block. Either way add a test that asserts the call SEQUENCE (spy on the three `ds.optimize.*` / `ds.cleanup_old_versions` entrypoints and assert the recorded order), so the invariant stops being prose.

findings.title: reconcile's load_sources awaits six independent stores sequentially where one asyncio.gather would do
COMPLETE lineage emits are awaited one-per-dataset inside the loop and uncapped, while the FAIL emits next to them are gathered AND capped for exactly that reason
findings.why: The stated hazard is symmetric but only half-mitigated. A first sweep over a freshly-migrated estate, or any tick after a large ingest, produces material work on many datasets at once; each COMPLETE publish is bounded at `publish_timeout_seconds` (default 5.0s, config.py:71), so N slow publishes cost 5N seconds serially with no ceiling — one hung sidecar and 7 datasets already exceeds the 30s window the FAIL path was capped to protect. Blowing the ack window makes Dapr redeliver the tick, which then hits the (racy, see MAINT-02) single-flight guard.
findings.recommendation: Collect the COMPLETE targets in the same single pass that already builds `failed` (the loop at :306 derives `(table_id, namespace)` for both branches anyway), then gather them with `return_exceptions=True` under the same `_MAX_FAIL_EMITS_PER_TICK`-style cap, logging what was dropped. That removes the asymmetry, halves the code, and makes one constant govern the tick's whole emit budget.

findings.title: Unguarded S3/Lance calls in the orphan category can raise out of reconcile() and 500 the entire tick, discarding the seven store categories that already succeeded
findings.why: This directly contradicts the module's stated design contract (reconcile.py:20-22): "a category whose source is unreachable reports UNAVAILABLE **with the reason** while the other six still report. A drift report that 500s on one bad store tells you nothing about the other six." Every other source in this file is funnelled through `_read_async`/`_read_blocking`, which convert failures to reason strings; the orphan category is the one that escapes. A single transient object-store error during the file scan therefore throws away a completed seven-category drift report, produces no `incomplete` entry naming what failed, and returns a 500 that makes Dapr redeliver the tick.
findings.recommendation: Wrap `_orphan_category`'s body the way every other source is wrapped: on failure append an `IncompleteScan(source="storage:datasets", reason=_reason(...))` and leave `orphan_files` absent from `counts` (so it reads as not-checked, never as zero — the module's own rule at :648). Inside `orphans.scan_dataset`, extend the existing `try` to cover `_unscannable_reason` so an unstattable prefix yields `checked=False` with a reason rather than escaping, and make `_unscannable_reason`'s `missing` comprehension raise-safe.

findings.title: The branch / MemWAL layout gate swallows its probe error and continues, failing OPEN on the one check that exists to stop live files being reported as garbage
findings.why: The comment justifies the swallow with "an unstattable path is not evidence of the layout" — true, but the safe conclusion from "I could not determine the layout" is REFUSE, not PROCEED. A transient S3 5xx or throttle on the `tree/` HEAD makes the only branch detector silently vanish and the dataset gets scanned as if it had no branches, producing exactly the false-positive class the module says it exists to prevent. That inverts the module's own doctrine, stated three times ("Layouts that make the method produce false positives on LIVE data. All are refused rather than approximated", :232; "a partial referenced-set would mark live files as orphans, the single most dangerous way this pass can be wrong", :97). It is currently contained only because orphan findings are report-only AND they inflate `report.total`, which blocks the #79 purge — a fail-closed accident, not a designed one; it becomes a data-loss path the day the orphan reclaimer this module is written for ships.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish "probed, absent" from "could not probe". Catch the error and return a refusal reason naming it (`f"{prefix}: could not probe for {directory}/ ({type(exc).__name__}: {exc}) — refusing rather than approximating the layout"`), which routes the dataset into the existing `checked=False` + `incomplete` path. If the false-refusal cost is judged too high on a flaky store, use pyarrow's batch `get_file_info([...])` for both probes so one call answers both, and still refuse on its failure.

findings.title: reconcile() builds a boto3 S3 client per call inside an async def when the lifespan-built client is absent — blocking construction on the event loop, and it silently defeats the documented UNAVAILABLE degradation
findings.why: Two rules broken and one contract silently reversed. (a) HOUSE-RULE-11/10: clients are built once in lifespan and injected — a per-call rebuild inside an `async def` runs boto3's session/model loading (disk IO + credential resolution) on the event loop every reconcile tick. (b) The documented degradation contract is bypassed: `dependencies.get_s3_client`, `service.py:148-150` ("a missing one degrades its categories to UNAVAILABLE-with-a-reason") and `_bucket_source` (reconcile.py:490) all promise that a missing S3 client makes `orphan_buckets` UNAVAILABLE — which, via `report_is_clean` (purge.py:191), BLOCKS the #79 purge. The hidden rebuild can flip that category from unavailable to checked, turning a report that was designed to refuse reclamation into one that permits it, through a code path nobody reading `service.py` or `dependencies.py` would know exists.
findings.recommendation: Delete the fallback. `reconcile()` should treat `bucket_client=None` as exactly what the dependency and the lifespan say it means, and let `_bucket_source` report the category unavailable. If a standalone (non-route) caller genuinely needs a client, have it build one and pass it in — the signature already accepts it. Same treatment for the `control_root` default (MAINT-08): make the callers supply the roots rather than re-deriving them here.

findings.title: reconcile()'s control_root default falls back to the POLICY root, not the control root — the exact root-confusion the sweep documents as a previously-invisible bug
findings.why: `_projects/`, `_warehouses/` and `_warehouses/bindings/` live on the CONTROL root; the reconciler reads them from whatever `resolved_control_root` resolves to. The two roots default to the same bucket, so — exactly as the sweep's comment warns — the defect is invisible until someone sets `MAINTENANCE_POLICY_ROOT`, at which point every registry listing comes back empty, every FGA tuple becomes a ghost, and the drift report is wrong estate-wide. It is a latent landmine rather than a live bug only because `routes.py:108` happens to pass `control_root=settings.resolved_control_root` explicitly — but `reconcile()` is a public function with a documented default, used directly by the tests, and the docstring actively teaches the wrong mapping.
findings.recommendation: Change the default to `settings.resolved_control_root` and fix the docstring to name `MAINTENANCE_CONTROL_ROOT`. Better still, drop the defaults entirely and make `control_root` a required keyword — the one production caller already passes it, and a reclamation-adjacent reader should not carry a silent root-resolution rule of its own. Add a unit test that sets `MAINTENANCE_POLICY_ROOT` to a different bucket than `MAINTENANCE_CONTROL_ROOT` and asserts the registries are read from the latter.

findings.title: run_sweep (172 lines) and compact_one (153 lines) are god-functions with 5-level nesting mixing discovery, registry reads, policy resolution, tracing, IO and metrics
findings.why: writing-python/design-patterns#function-size: extract at 20-50 lines, at multiple purposes, or at 3+ nesting levels — all three are exceeded, in the two functions that rewrite and delete lakehouse data. The concrete cost is visible in the code itself: the policy-extraction block and its `except` twin at :214-220 duplicate the default set, which is why the comment there has to explain that the recovery path must not silently become unbounded — a hazard that only exists because defaults are written twice in one function.
findings.recommendation: Split `run_sweep` into named steps it already has comments for: `_load_policies(settings, options)`, `_resolve_sweep_buckets(settings, options)` (config + registry), `_discover_all(fs, buckets)` → `(uris, truncated)`, `_report_due_trash(...)`, and `_maintain_one(uri, policy_records, settings, options, now) -> DatasetResult` holding the span + policy resolution + `compact_one` + stamp. Replace the six-field `if policy.get(...)` ladder with a small Pydantic `ResolvedPolicy` model built by one `from_record(policy, settings)` classmethod — that also collapses the duplicated default set in the `except`. In `compact_one`, lift the `defer_index_remap` fallback into `_compact_with_fallback(ds, size_kw, uri)` and the version-reclamation branch into `_reclaim_versions(ds, result, ...)`.

findings.title: build_report repeats the same guard/else block seven times, and two categories pass the same reason pair to _first in opposite order
findings.why: The category name is written twice per block (once in `CategoryUnavailable`, once as the `counts` key) and the field name twice more, so adding an eighth category means four places to keep in sync and nothing checks them — the `CATEGORIES` tuple at :85 already exists as the intended single list but is not used to drive this. The `_first` order inconsistency has no functional effect today (both branches produce a reason string) but it means two categories can report DIFFERENT reasons for the identical failure, which is confusing precisely when an operator is triaging why the #79 purge is blocked.
findings.recommendation: Drive the loop from a table: a list of `(name, field, error_reasons_callable, detector_callable)` rows — or a small Pydantic `CategorySpec` — iterated once, so category name, target field and count key are each written exactly once and `CATEGORIES` becomes the derived source of truth rather than a parallel constant. Normalise `_first`'s argument order per input pair while you are there.

findings.title: core/lance_trace.py is a 217-line module with zero callers and zero tests, plus an unused constant in orphans.py
findings.why: The module carries a documented process-global, panic-on-double-registration side effect (`capture_trace_events` — "A SECOND `capture_trace_events` call **panics**", :30) and a `BaseException` catch strategy built around it, none of which has ever executed in this codebase. Shipping an untested global-state installer that nothing calls is the worst of both: it costs review attention, it claims to be the judge of the #102 shared-session fix ("Without them the cache fix is unfalsifiable in prod", :8) while providing exactly zero signal, and the first person to wire it up will be its first tester. writing-python/anti-patterns F4/G9: if it's not called, delete it — git remembers.
findings.recommendation: Pick one: either wire it into the lifespan behind a `MAINTENANCE_LANCE_TRACE_ENABLED` setting (with the chart env row and at least one unit test driving `LanceTraceRecorder` against an in-memory metric reader — the class was explicitly split out to make that possible, :71-74), or delete the file. Do not leave it in the tree unwired. Delete `_VERSION_HINT` or use it in the filter at orphans.py:342 so the comment and the code agree.

findings.title: The multi-base layout gate issues one sequential S3 HEAD per referenced path with no batching and no short-circuit, on every dataset in every bucket
findings.why: For a compacted table with a long history this is thousands of individual, sequential `HEAD` round-trips against RustFS/S3 per dataset, multiplied by every dataset in every configured and registry-discovered bucket — inside a scan whose own docstring already calls itself "a different order of work" (reconcile.py:645). pyarrow's `get_file_info` accepts a LIST of paths and issues them concurrently; the single-path form in a comprehension throws that away. It also cannot short-circuit: even when the first path is missing (the answer is already decided) it stats every remaining path. Each of those calls is additionally an unguarded raise point (see MAINT-05).
findings.recommendation: Replace with the batch form: `infos = fs.get_file_info([f"{prefix}/{rel}" for rel in exact_matches])`, then zip against the path list to find the missing ones. That is one call, concurrent inside pyarrow, and gives the same `len(missing)` / `missing[0]` output. If a full answer is not needed, iterate lazily and break on the first miss — the message only needs one example.

findings.title: Routes are registered at import time from a module-level get_settings(), with tags on each route instead of the APIRouter
docs_enabled defaults to True and the chart never sets it false, so /docs and /openapi.json are served in production despite the comment claiming otherwise

Identity drift left over from the compaction→maintenance rename: a wire-visible OpenLineage producer URI pointing at a path and repo that no longer exist, and a metric namespace that still says compaction
Helpers with 4-5 positional parameters and functions that mutate a caller-owned report/output argument in place
Gateway rebuilds the upstream URL from the percent-DECODED path, corrupting or truncating it (and 500-ing on some inputs)
findings.why: A proxy must forward the path the caller sent. Here the gateway routes and 403-guards on the full decoded path but hands the upstream a DIFFERENT, shorter one — so a request can be authorized against one resource and executed against another. `%1F` is worse than wrong: `httpx.InvalidURL` is not a `RequestError`, so it misses the 502 handler at line 330 and escapes as an unhandled 500 from wholly client-controlled input. The Lance Namespace spec's canonical identifier delimiter is the unit separator (rask's catalog currently configures `$` via LANCE_NS_DELIMITER, which is what keeps this latent rather than live), and any path parameter carrying an encoded '/', '?' or '#' — annotator doc/speech/chunk ids, future object keys — hits the truncation today.
findings.recommendation: Route on `_normalize_path(request.url.path)` as now, but BUILD the upstream URL from `request.scope["raw_path"]` (falling back to the encoded form of `request.url.path`) so the wire path round-trips byte-for-byte: slice the raw bytes by the raw-prefix length rather than the decoded one, and construct with `httpx.URL(base).copy_with(raw_path=...)` instead of f-string concatenation, which re-parses ':', '?' and '#' as delimiters. Add `httpx.InvalidURL` to the guarded exceptions so a malformed identifier is a 400, never a 500. Pin all four reproductions above as tests.

findings.title: Caller-supplied regex is compiled and executed on the event loop — a `regex` node freezes the whole flows process
findings.why: `/api/*` has no auth in front of it (documented: "No auth, no app middleware"), so one `POST /api/flows/runs` with a 40-character seed takes the flows pod out until the liveness probe kills it — and `/api/health` is `async def` on the same frozen loop, so the probe fails too. `alto_lines`'s `.*?`-DOTALL scan (line 117) and `compare_texts` are the same class of unbounded CPU work in the same async path, just without an attacker-chosen exponent.
findings.recommendation: Run every pure-CPU node arm off the loop — `await run_in_threadpool(...)` (or `asyncio.to_thread`) inside the `regex`/`alto`/`compare`/`extract` arms of `dispatch` — and bound the regex itself: cap the subject length, and either reject nested-quantifier patterns or move the match behind an `asyncio.wait_for` on a thread. A thread does not stop the GIL stall, so the length cap is the load-bearing half. `re` alternatives with linear-time guarantees (`google-re2`) are the durable fix if user regex stays a product feature.

findings.title: `run_node` catches only `NodeError`, so a bad `regexReplace` 500s the entire run and orphans its sibling nodes
findings.why: The stated contract of this module is "failure captured as state rather than raised" so the builder can paint one node red — a design `test_a_failing_model_node_blocks_its_dependents` asserts explicitly. Any exception that is not a `NodeError` silently violates it, and `regexReplace` is a plain text field in the published catalog, so this is reachable by typing. `asyncio.gather` without `return_exceptions=True` also leaves the wave's other node coroutines running detached with their results discarded and their in-flight Serve POSTs still open. On the durable lane the same escape raises out of the activity, burns all three `NODE_RETRY` attempts on a deterministic failure, and then fails the whole workflow.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the substitution in the same `except re.error -> NodeError` guard the compile already has, and make the escape structurally impossible: broaden `run_node`'s handler to `except Exception as exc` — logging it at exception level and returning a failed `NodeRunState` with a stable message — since a node failing is a normal outcome and an unexpected exception inside one node must not be able to abort the run. Pass `return_exceptions=True` to the `gather` so a wave always resolves.

findings.title: 19 raw `os.environ` reads outside any settings module — the gateway has no Settings class at all, and several reads happen per request
findings.why: `service_kit.config.Settings` already declares `api_prefix` (RASK_API_PREFIX), `dapr_enabled` (RASK_DAPR_ENABLED) and `dapr_http_port` (DAPR_HTTP_PORT) with the exact same aliases, and gateway already depends on `service-kit` — so these are re-implementations of fields the estate owns, with no validation and no single read point. Concrete hazards, not style: (a) `_routes()` calls `load_dotenv()` and line 257 does not, so the two RASK_API_PREFIX reads agree only because line 256 happens to run first — reorder them and the routing prefix silently diverges from the openapi/docs prefix; (b) `int(os.environ.get(...))` at import turns a typo'd `RASK_PRUNE_KEEP_JOBS` into a bare `ValueError` during module import instead of a pydantic-settings validation error at startup, and bakes the binding route path in so it cannot be overridden per deployment or exercised in a test.
findings.recommendation: Give the gateway a `GatewaySettings(BaseSettings)` (RASK_* aliases, one field per upstream, `lru_cache`d), build it once in the lifespan onto `app.state.settings`, and derive `_routes()`/`_target_base()`/the blocklist from it — the per-request env reads then become attribute lookups. Move `RASK_PRUNE_BINDING`/`RASK_PRUNE_KEEP_JOBS` into a compute settings model read in `make_lifespan`, and `RASK_PROJECT_URL_SCHEME` into a controlplane one injected via `SettingsDep`.

findings.title: `/openapi.json` fetches ten backends sequentially with a 10 s timeout each — worst case ~100 s on a client-facing request
findings.why: These fetches are entirely independent — the canonical `asyncio.gather` case. In a partially-deployed estate (the chart's own `frontDoor: true` front-door-only install is an explicitly supported mode) every absent backend costs a full connect timeout in series, so the gateway's own `/docs` becomes a ~100 s hang. Sequentially awaiting independent I/O is the concurrency rule, and here it is a user-visible latency cliff rather than a micro-optimisation.
findings.recommendation: `results = await asyncio.gather(*(_fetch_spec(client, base, prefix) for base in bases), return_exceptions=True)`, merging in the original target order so the result stays deterministic. Drop the per-target timeout to ~2 s once they run concurrently.

findings.title: The 502 body prints the internal upstream address to the public caller — the exact leak `_rewrite_location` exists to prevent
findings.why: The gateway is the only listener exposed to the public ingress; everything behind it is an internal name. Handing an anonymous caller the service DNS names, ports, and (with Dapr enabled) the sidecar invoke topology is free reconnaissance, and it directly contradicts the module's own stated rule. `flows/executor.py:372` shows the estate already knows the right shape — it names the CONFIGURED address, not the resolved one, and only the exception class.
findings.recommendation: Log the full detail (`log.warning("upstream unreachable", extra={"app_id": app_id, "base": base, "error": str(exc)})`) and return a body that names only the public route: `detail=f"upstream for {route_prefix} is unreachable"`. Same treatment for the 404 at line 318, which echoes the raw request path back.

findings.title: The gateway is the only service in the fleet that does not answer RFC 9457 problem+json
findings.why: The gateway is the single origin every generated client talks to, so its 403/404/502 are the errors clients see MOST — and they arrive in a different content type and shape from every error the same client gets when the upstream is up. A client written against problem+json (the catalog's generated client dispatches on the numeric code) has to carry a second parser purely for the edge.
findings.recommendation: Call `service_kit.exceptions.register_handlers(app)` and raise the shared `NotFoundError` / `ServiceUnavailableError` (or a small `BadGatewayError`) instead of bare `HTTPException`; return the 403 guard through the same hierarchy. That also fixes the internal-address leak above for free, since `_problem` serialises only the stable `detail`.

findings.title: Every proxied request body is fully buffered in memory, though responses are correctly streamed
findings.why: `await request.body()` materialises the entire upload before a single byte reaches the upstream. The gateway fronts `/api/ingest` (the ingest control plane), `/api/explorer/annotations` (the annotator's Arrow-IPC writes) and `/api/produce` — the three planes whose payloads are the least bounded. A handful of concurrent large POSTs multiply straight into the pod's memory limit, and the buffering also adds full-upload latency before the upstream sees anything. The asymmetry with the response path shows the streaming primitive was already understood here.
findings.recommendation: Pass `content=request.stream()` to `build_request` so the body is proxied as an async byte iterator, and drop `content-length` handling to httpx. Keep the buffered path only if some route genuinely needs to re-read the body — none in this file does.

findings.title: The merged OpenAPI silently drops colliding paths — every service's `/api/health` overwrites the previous one
Route rows are positional 4-tuples read by index, and `_merged_openapi` returns a bare `dict`
A durable run reports `running` forever — the workflow's terminal state is never read back into `GET /flows/runs/{id}`
findings.why: The routes' own comment defers *streaming per-node progress*, which is a reasonable v0 cut; the terminal status is a different thing and is not covered by that deferral. As it stands the durable lane — the lane whose entire purpose is surviving a crash — is strictly less observable than the inline one: a caller can never learn that a run succeeded, failed, or died. Two compounding facts, both currently masked by `chart/values.yaml:190` pinning `replicas: 1`: the store is per-process (stated honestly at dependencies.py:25-33) so scheduling on one replica and polling another 404s, and `_remember`'s `max_runs` eviction can drop a still-`running` durable row while its workflow is alive.
findings.recommendation: In `get_run`, when the stored state is `running` and a scheduler is present, call `get_workflow_state(instance_id=run_id)` off the loop (`asyncio.to_thread` + a timeout, as `DaprFlowScheduler.schedule` already does) and project `runtime_status` / `serialized_output` onto the response, refreshing the cached row on a terminal status. That makes the workflow history the record — which is what `dependencies.get_runs` already argues it should be — rather than adding a second writer. Record the single-replica constraint on the chart entry until it does.

findings.title: Two unbounded `except Exception` blocks make a code defect indistinguishable from an absent sidecar
findings.why: A `NameError`, a bad `@wfr.activity` signature, a Pydantic model error or a missing transitive dependency inside `flows/workflow.py` is caught here and reported as "dapr workflow runtime unavailable", at WARNING, on a service that then boots green and runs every flow inline forever. That is the failure mode the estate has already paid for once — `test_workflow.py`'s own docstring records ingest shipping a deploy whose sidecar said `Workflow engine started` while the app had registered nothing, "an asymmetry that looks healthy from every angle except an actual run." The `except Exception` at routes.py:98 has the same shape (it is at least logged at exception level and the comment names a measured cause), and lifespan.py:82 swallows shutdown failures.
findings.recommendation: Split the block: do the import unguarded (an import error is a build defect and should crash-loop honestly, exactly as the chart's `waitFor: []` allows), and guard only `wfr.start()` — narrowing to the gRPC/connection exception types `dapr-ext-workflow` actually raises. Surface the resulting lane on `/health` or a startup metric so "durable expected, inline actual" is visible without reading logs.

findings.title: `create_run` hand-builds a problem+json body and returns `RunState | JSONResponse` because the shared exception hierarchy cannot carry extension members
The Serve proxy forwards `content-encoding`/`content-length` from an upstream body httpx has already decompressed
findings.why: httpx sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` by default and the browser's own accept-encoding is forwarded through `dict(request.headers)`, so any compressed response from the Ray dashboard is served to the SPA as gzip-labelled plaintext with a length 2× off. The browser then fails to inflate it or truncates the JSON, and the `/serve` page breaks in a way that looks like a dashboard fault. Note the same module gets the equivalent right on the request side (`host`, `authorization`, `cookie` all stripped) — this is a gap in one set, not a missing concept.
findings.recommendation: Add `content-encoding` and `content-length` to `_RESPONSE_STRIP` (Starlette then computes the correct length for the decoded body), or forward `resp.aiter_raw()` and keep both headers. Same review for `content-length` on the request side once anything but GET/HEAD is proxied.

findings.title: `get_ray_client` re-runs the blocking `build_client` on every request while Ray is down, with no backoff or negative caching
findings.why: `JobSubmissionClient` construction performs a synchronous connection check (`requests`, its own timeout). While Ray is down — which the comment itself says can be "minutes, on a fresh cluster" — every request to `/ray/health`, `/ray/jobs` and the prune cron occupies a threadpool slot for a full connect timeout. Starlette's threadpool is 40 workers shared with every other sync route in the process, so a Ray outage degrades unrelated endpoints. `test_get_ray_client_rebuilds_lazily_when_none` pins the rebuild but not its cost.
findings.recommendation: Keep the lazy rebuild but rate-limit it: store the last attempt time on `app.state` and skip the rebuild for a cooldown (e.g. 10 s), returning `None` immediately in between — the endpoints already render an honest `ok=False` for that. A `tenacity` retry with `stop_after_delay` around the lifespan build plus the cooldown here centralises the policy in one place, per the resilience rule.

findings.title: The controlplane's designed 503 cannot fire for its likeliest cause — `load_kube_config()` raises inside the dependency, outside the route's try
findings.why: "No kubeconfig and not in-cluster" is the single most common way this service fails (any local run, any pod whose ServiceAccount token is not mounted), and it is the one case `_K8S_ERRORS` names explicitly. The intended answer is a clean 503 the home picker can render as "control plane unavailable"; the actual answer is a 500 with a traceback. `lru_cache` does not cache exceptions, so it retries — and 500s — on every request. The test suite injects a fake reader through `dependency_overrides`, which is precisely the path that bypasses this construction, so nothing catches it.
findings.recommendation: Move the failure into the guarded region: have `get_reader` return a lazily-connecting reader (construct the k8s clients on first `list_projects()` call), or wrap the dependency itself so a `ConfigException` becomes `ServiceUnavailableError`. While there, raise `service_kit.exceptions.ServiceUnavailableError` rather than a bare `HTTPException` — the module's own docstring says routes raise those "never `HTTPException` directly", and it is what makes this 503 problem+json like every other error the app emits. Add a test that lets the real `K8sProjectReader` construction fail.

findings.title: One blocking Kubernetes API call per project to resolve ingress hosts, where one cluster-wide call would do
findings.why: `GET /api/projects/` costs 1 + N serialized blocking API calls, so the home picker's latency grows linearly with the number of projects and each one holds a threadpool slot for the duration. The selector is already the same for every namespace, which is the tell: `list_ingress_for_all_namespaces(label_selector="platform.rask.io/project")` answers the whole question in one request. It also makes the endpoint fail partially in a way nothing reports — one slow namespace stalls the entire list.
findings.recommendation: Add a `list_project_ingress_hosts() -> dict[str, str]` to the `ProjectReader` protocol backed by `list_ingress_for_all_namespaces(label_selector=...)`, build the namespace→host map once, and have `list_project_dtos` look up rather than call. Keeps `service.py` pure and drops the request to two API calls regardless of project count.

findings.title: Kubernetes CRs are walked as `dict[str, Any]` with `.get()` chains instead of validated at the boundary
`lines` is forwarded unbounded to the Ray dashboard; both it and `tail` are declared without `Annotated[..., Query(...)]`
`compute/tests/conftest.py` mutates `os.environ` at import, leaking into every other suite in the session
Write authorship comes from an unverified, client-supplied `X-User` header
findings.why: Any caller who can reach the annotator can attribute an annotation write to an arbitrary principal by setting one header. In a national-archive system the author stamp is the provenance record; a forgeable one silently corrupts the audit trail and any downstream review/attribution query, and it does so invisibly (the write succeeds, FGA passes, nothing logs an anomaly). The verified subject the service already computes makes this a wiring gap, not a missing capability.
findings.recommendation: Make the write paths depend on the verified subject: in the annotator, replace `author: AuthorDep` with `author: CurrentSubject` on `save_annotations` and the tags route. In service-kit, either delete `get_author`/`AuthorDep` or narrow it to read-only surfaces and rename it so the trust level is in the name (e.g. `UntrustedAuthorDep`); better, move the seam into `service_kit.governed` so the shared kit exposes exactly one identity dep and the header path cannot be reached from a governed service. If the header must survive for dev, gate it on an explicit `auth disabled` setting rather than on its own absence.

findings.title: `LocalCatalogWriteTransport` (dev/offline catalog fallback) omits the commit-conflict translation the direct path has — 500 instead of 409
findings.why: A reachable configuration silently reverts a fixed correctness bug. On the in-process catalog fallback an ordinary optimistic-concurrency loss surfaces as an unmapped 500 rather than the 409 the annotator client is written to handle, so the user's annotation delta is discarded instead of being rebuilt and merged — data loss on the exact path the OCC machinery exists to protect. The three write methods are also byte-identical to `LanceTableWriter`'s bodies minus the wrapper, so the divergence is pure copy-paste drift with no design intent behind it.
findings.recommendation: Have `LocalCatalogWriteTransport` delegate to `LanceTableWriter` (`self._w = LanceTableWriter(ds)`; each method forwards) so there is one implementation of the three Lance calls and one place the conflict translation lives. Add a test mirroring `tests/test_commit_conflict.py` that drives the local-catalog transport, so the two paths cannot drift again.

findings.title: A fresh urllib3 `ApiClient` is constructed per catalog read/write call and never closed
findings.why: Every catalog-backed read or write pays a fresh TCP (and, in prod, TLS) handshake instead of reusing a pooled connection — the ~10x-slowdown pattern the house rules call out by name — and a single `save_annotations` request builds TWO of them (reader at :78, writer at :116). The pools are also never explicitly released, so their teardown depends on refcount timing rather than a lifespan. This is precisely the resource the app factory's lifespan seam exists to own.
findings.recommendation: Build one `ApiClient` per app in the lifespan, stash it on `app.state` (or on the `AppState` resource bag next to `http`), and change `RestCatalogTransport`/`RestCatalogWriteTransport` to accept an already-built `DataApi`/`ApiClient` rather than a base URL. Keep `open_reader`/`open_writer` as the selection seam but have them take the shared client via a dep. Close it in the lifespan's post-`yield`. The per-caller bearer token can move from `set_default_header` to a per-request header argument so one client still serves every caller.

findings.title: Errors are classified by substring-matching exception messages in three separate places
findings.why: Three independent, undocumented dependencies on pylance's English error prose. A wording change in a Lance upgrade flips a 404 into a 500 (or, worse, lets a permission/IO error match `"not found"` and be reported as a missing table, hiding a real outage behind a routine-looking 404). The writer module is honest that no typed error exists (`writer.py:49-52`), but the two reader/registry sites make the same bet without saying so, and none of the three is pinned by a test against the installed pylance's actual messages except the commit-conflict one.
findings.recommendation: Centralize the classification in one module (e.g. `lancekit/lance_errors.py`) exposing `is_not_found(exc)` / `is_commit_conflict(exc)` with the marker tuples as module constants, so there is one vocabulary and one place to fix on a pylance bump — the same consolidation `writer.py` already argues for in its `_COMMIT_CONFLICT_MARKERS` comment. Add a test per predicate that asserts against a real pylance-raised error (not a hand-built `OSError`) so a version bump reddens CI instead of silently changing status codes.

findings.title: A transient per-table read failure is laundered into a 404 "dataset not found"
findings.why: An S3 blip, an expired credential or a mid-rebuild table makes one `table_info` call fail; the chain then tells the client the dataset's row table "does not exist" and answers 404. Operators see no 5xx, no alert and no error-rate signal — a storage outage renders as an empty/not-found corpus. The comment at `state.py:90` asserts the ValueError is always "a config problem", but `discover_tables`' bare `except Exception` guarantees it is not.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish absent from unreadable: have `discover_tables` catch only the not-found classification (see SK-04) and let anything else propagate, or record unreadable tables in a separate `unreadable: dict[str, str]` on the result so `validate_descriptor` can say "unreadable" rather than "does not exist". Split the descriptor failure into two exception types — a `DescriptorInvalidError` (config, → 404/422) and a `DatasetUnavailableError` (transport, → 503) — and map them separately in `dataset_handle` so an outage surfaces as `ServiceUnavailableError`.

findings.title: The dataset registry is lazily built inside request handling, unguarded, and the handles are never released
findings.why: Two distinct costs.
